game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Don't mind my playtime, I've played and finished this game on another platform so it's not counted here.
I can absolutely say that this game is very brilliant. From the UI design which makes you feel like you're really working from home on your own computer, to the story, which is very well written and developed.

The more you go on with the story, if you really pay attention to the details, the more the plot twist becames obvious, but it's certainly nothing you might expect from the beginning.

It's kinda short, and if you're not a fan of the genre it might be a little boring, since the things you do, except for those you can decide on, are actually driven and highlited by the game itself, so the interaction is almost limited to what the game wants you to do, but again, if you like the genre, the main feature of this game is actually the story, and the fact that you can discover it only bit by bit, by reading all the information given.

Currently this game is on sale, together with the second one in a bundle, and for less more than 4€ is totally a must-buy.

Small digression on the translation: I played the game with the Italian translation because that's my main language, the game started automatically in that language and it seemed ok in the beginning.
Sadly, the more it goes on, the more it gets worse. Some translated sentences are even totally senseless and sometimes it gets a little frustrating to read, since the game is based on reading info.
I understand that even if it's very bad it might be useful for people who can't read English, but I only wish I had a way to switch to English language in-game, so that I could have changed language while playing.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
TL:DR, I myself enjoyed this game, great if you are into detective type work. Not a super exciting but overall 7/10

For the record, I got this while on sale for 5 dollars during steam sales. I see normally priced at 10 and that would be a maybe for buying it. 

So by the title you can guess that this has to do with big brother type surveillance, but in this you are acting as the investigator using the big brother program aka Orwell as a tool to piece together the story as it is happening about a alleged terrorist group. I can definitely see where someone could play this and find it dull and boring, but for me personally I found it intriguing and fun being able to access files and eavesdrop on conversation and collect intel from all sources. As well as building up character profiles and finding the relationships. One of few complaints I have is the moral dillema is kinda thrown in your face in the last moments of the game, which didn't ruin the game for me because it does then offer you a choice, but just felt very uninspired in a sense. The story leading to it was all around pretty good. While character development was great at times and very stereotypical in other times, the act of putting together character history and connections is actual quite fun. Especially in a sense where going through my first play through seemed to not matter and as though it seemed straight forward, looking at the achievements afterward and noticing I am missing half of them. And looking at the details of the achievements I can see where my actions can affect the story through the game. Similar to the character development, the story plot points were mostly good, but lack luster in other times. 

Gameplay itself feels immersive to me, but dont go into this expecting a whole bunch of mechanics or crazy things you can do. You are essentially sitting on a computer screen doing research and hacking into things. 

I will say, I went into this expecting there to be different cases as well, not to say I was dissapointed, I just thought there would be more to the game itself.

For 5 bucks and the first run through taking only 3 hours to complete I would recommend it, and I might go through again to see if I can knock out the other achievements and to really see what affect I have on the game.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What would you do if you really wanted to imprison some people that irked you? Obviously, you would scour their Facebook, Twitter, and eHarmony profiles to gather evidence of corroboration between them and terrorist activist cells. Atleast that’s how Osmotic Studios would do it. Although it may be a bit of a crude hyperbole, that is essentially what you will be doing in Orwell, the fascinating game where you play as Big Brother in an effort to keep The Nation safe and discover the culprits behind the recent bombing events in the capital city.

[h1]Privacy vs Security[/h1]

Other than being the author of 1984, the story where this game gets many of its motifs from, Orwell is rebirthed as a new governmental security program created to maintain order and reduce crime in a totalitarian country called, The Nation. Being an all-encompassing program with no bounds in breaking personal privacy, Orwell has the ability to retrieve: medical records, user submitted online information, bank statements, school records, mobile device data, telephone calls, chat room conversations, and pc device data. Your role in ensuring the safety of The Nation is in the capacity of an investigator, one who has authority to utilize the Orwell mainframe as an unbiased outsider to The Nation. As an investigator, you must sift through all of the information Orwell retrieves to discover and submit “relevant” datachunks to your immediate supervisor. What you deem relevant will shape the futures of the suspects under investigation, so take great care in deciding what to submit to Orwell.

Gameplay-wise, Orwell’s UI behaves much like an internet browser with three major utilities: the Reader, Listener, and Insider. These utilities allow you to pull up internet-related articles, tap into phone calls or chat conversations, or remote control mobile/PC devices respectively. Throughout the countless scripts of text provided by the articles or conversations, datachunks are automatically highlighted, and notifications beside specific entries where datachunks are present help guide the player towards progression. Some datachunks will be relatively useless, such as a person’s favorite color, but others will be extremely relevant to the case. Chunk by chunk, you will eventually develop fully-fleshed profiles to aid you in determining who the next person of interest is until the final culprit is found.

[h1]License to Know[/h1]

Using Orwell's features is the crux of the game, letting you slowly form your own opinion on who may be innocent or an accomplice, all while unraveling deeper motivations about the suspects and influential figures around you and Orwell. When you think you've cleanly profiled someone, post-incident reports will reveal multiple perspectives with conflicting beliefs that you may have never even thought of. As each episode focuses on a different character, everyone feels really well developed and sharply defined by disparate personalities and lifestyles. In addition, the more you learn about one thing, the less confident you will feel about another. 

Although the detective aspect of the game begins off strong, it unfortunately slowly undermines itself due to the fact that every clue is essentially hand-fed to the player. Since notifications of datachunks are provided, what ended up seeming to be a neat and helpful feature to ensure that I can progress without too much trouble began to feel like a massive crutch. This created an extremely casual playstyle where I was really just along for the ride. Don't get me wrong, it is still one great journey, but the immersiveness could have been kicked up a notch by providing players a serious investigative challenge. For example, if all notifications and highlighted entries were removed, it would definitely force me to care much more about the seemingly mundane or extraneous text for fear of relevancy. Finding the clues could be as "simple" as manually highlighting useful data. The supervisor continued to nag me about looking for X, finding X, learning more about X, but eventually the clues led me there without trying anyways. I felt like I might as well just speed-read anything without highlighted text in it to quickly move on. 

In addition, certain clues must be fed to Orwell to proceed, even if I wanted to exclude it. The game seems to make a big deal about being careful what to upload to the mainframe, so why force me to make choices like that. Maybe I'm inclined to believe X is innocent, but to proceed, I must upload information that X has a military background in order to create clearance for investigation. Having this feature further supports the casual mindset of submitting anything that is highlighted and diminishes the need to read everything or even care. Don’t get me wrong, the game still provides the players with a fair amount of control, since the endings are vastly different and minor paths will affect the outcome of certain suspects, but I definitely did not welcome the need to have milestone/checkpoint datachunks for progression.

The datachunk system still has some pretty neat features though, most notably in regards to data conflicts. At these moments, two conflicting statements are uncovered and only one can be submitted. You will essentially provide info that you want your supervisor to act upon. Ex. "I heard X was home last night....[phone conversation]" vs "Me and X had a blast at the concert last night [social networking site]." What you choose will relatively dictate what will happen to X. These conflicts returned a little bit of control taken away with the abovementioned checkpoint chunks.

[h1]Complete Walkthrough Playlist[/h1]

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s6Q75R9yWtU&list=PLeavCsRFiP55ATTks7hLjJY84dnSIXY3y&index=1

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

At first, Orwell seemed to have been just a more interactive visual novel or point & click game, but certain scripted scenes suddenly thrust me into Orwell's world, making me experience the exact same feelings a tech-savvy security investigator would be facing. Times where I would suddenly lose access to Orwell's mainframe, experience a cyber-attack, discover life-threatening secrets or aid Orwell during an active escape attempt. I found myself making motions and exasperations my virtual counterpart would most likely make, and the intense emotions I felt during these moments are something that would be highly difficult to forget as I walk away from the game. I can't recall any visual novels or point & clicks that have made me feel so involved in its world, seemingly shaping the final conclusion to the story.

Even though I have some gripes with Orwell’s progression and datachunk systems, the game is a far cry from being a failure at its attempt to tell a captivating story with novel methods. It isn’t easy for a game to present information in such a way to draw strong opinions from the players, yet manage to continually make their beliefs sway back and forth. The developers, however, knew how to create false trails, dead ends, probable causes and multiple motivations yet skew them towards a believable conclusion. Furthermore, scripted moments that nearly broke the fourth wall created a unique sense of immersion and relatability. This makes it very easy for me to recommend Orwell to any fan of story-centric narratives or spy games. If you’re still on the fence about this game, try the demo. It is free and contains the entire first episode - and it only gets better from there.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The creation of the internet is the most technological advance tool mankind has ever made, right next to toilets. With the modern age of technology we have today, the effects on our lives stack up as the age-old question Security vs. Freedom comes into the debate again.  I am talking about a game where it tackles the subject on privacy issues which is Orwell. There will be a spoiler section on the comments to give my personal thoughts on some episodes. I will give an analytical review of this game and give in my two cents if this plays well as it was intended. 

[h1]CHECKING YOUR ID[/h1]

You play as Snowden-I MEAN the investigator, you work for the government and try a new technology called Orwell. You checked on people’s devices and try to add data chunks that matter on a case you are specifically working on. To be frank, in the first episode I was intrigued by the concept of the machine, it felt the game was really inspired by the true story of Edward Snowden about the CIA scandal. Now, the difference from the actual real event and the game is that the game focus on only the investigator and your co-worker trying to solve this case together. You the investigator only see the dirty secrets while your advisor Symes only advice you on your next tasks or comment on your search. I will explain a bit more detail but it will have to be in the spoiler section on why Orwell works like that.

[h1]BACKGROUND CHARACTERS AND STORY[/h1]

I have to cut a lot to avoid spoilers so I will give you a summary of the story but will give you how the characters and their world behave. The story is interesting for how it was trying to show the concept of privacy. I absolutely love how each character from the profiles you investigate shows a unique dialogue from each text you read from different characters. They feel almost exactly like how people should talk especially on the internet. When you read each email, phone calls etc. you can picture actual people having a real conversation which is great! It never made you feel like the dialogue felt artificial or fake, like adults “trying” to sound what people would say on the internet. I also love how they try to implement how people would sound like on the comment sections and insert memes along the way. 

The art style is another unique aspect of the game of how it shows a polygonal art style look. Most of the faces are fine though some were not as quite good in certain looks like some faces of the characters you profile are a bit strange with their beady eyes or mouth. The music is quite good giving you a sense of futuristic vibe to it while also gives you a dread feeling where certain events happen during your case. You even have one shot whatever you send data chunks to Symes and you can’t go back to it even exit the game won’t do. Whatever you send to Symes will affect the characters that you are working on the case. Which now I will talk about the actual meat of the review, the concept of the game and the driving point of Orwell.

[h1] THE CHOICE IS YOURS[/h1]

The focus of what the developers are getting at is the whole anti-surveillance vs. freedom. The story hints you that the Nation (that is the country of this game) is trying to add more cameras after the safety bill was passed and some foreign problem that led to mass immigration, based on what the articles within the game said. The game even tried to give you signs that you are “supposedly” working for the bad guy and that the group that you were assigned to follow name [i]Thought[/i] is the good guys because they believe in Freedom of Speech and you are trying to incriminate them. How exactly you are incriminating them is because of how Orwell is set up to be. Orwell is a super-computer that analyze information and even interpret the information for you to post it. Unfortunately, because of how Orwell acts according to its programming it will translate the language the program will find it logical. Which leads to falsify the context that was given if you don’t read their messages clearly because remember, only you know the truth and Symes is only there as your advisor so he won’t know the full context of your side of the truth, only Orwell.  That is why it can be easy for people to get arrested just because Symes read what you send base on Orwell translated. Is this good?

 Well at first I almost had a problem with It because why the developers put it that way, but later as I finished the game I realized this was purposefully done this way and it was the right call. The purpose of their message is that people have way too much confidence of a machine to do their jobs for you they forgot how machines can be the dumbest tools for interpreting human language which they probably will never understand unless you are human. This is why in real life there are moderators to keep track of reports of people saying certain stuff. Bots can detect it but when humans actually read the context of their side of the story the problem is fix. The game did a great job of showing how humans rely on Orwell too much, but what I’m most impress is why they design the game to make it only you see the whole truth. 

In my playthrough I played the game like it was real life, I pretend I actually worked for the government and I role-play as an investigator, although sometimes I break my role to send certain data chunks that have nothing to do with the case but to pull Symes hair on certain funny comments. Anyway, when you sit down and do your “job” to be the eye on everyone’s business, not to joke around I felt pressure on taking the responsibility on sending people’s privacy, even if it means breaking some moral codes for the good of saving lives. I somehow felt like a god knowing people’s secrets and manipulate their lives on sending whatever data it comes and I send that data to Symes so that he take action to do something of this person. I can see why having this kind of power is utter madness to have, but at the same time is it really crazy to have this power?

 The game gives you a clear sense of black and white of giving you choices to follow, either be pro-government by pleasing them everything you send or follow your own thoughts of which is good and bad. Certainly, nobody here is good at least for the group [i]Thought[/i], I wish Symes would talk more of his stance of the government trying to make people safe like he would talk about how certain parts of giving up freedom for security is good even if they don’t understand. This would create an even more dilemma which the game has but certain parts fail which leads to my last discussion. 

How it handles the 1984 concepts. I felt they only scratch the surface of what it truly means for giving up your freedom. [i]Thought[/i] members tell you how bad cameras but they don’t know how the cameras are being used, they just say is bad because of privacy reasons. One member says they love the freedom of speech but at the same time I don’t see the government censoring their citizenships, maybe their newspaper but nothing more am I missing something? I heard they have immigration problem so why not show more articles showing the effects of the safety bill. Are they discriminate more by taking away their privacy than the Nation’s citizens?

 Do the immigrants have the same freedom as the Nation?  These are questions they sort of tell but just not the amount where the players really ask themselves if freedom does have a cost or that if security has its perk for saving citizens, where is the line on that. To me, it felt like a basic philosophy lesson about Orwellian which does not go as deep as I thought.  

In the end is still a great game to start with the season, the concept is interesting and even the certain parts of the game felt too real of how our world functions in terms of responding of cameras everywhere. This game deserves a 7/10! Recommend for a good short time experience for a fan of dystopian settings.

[i]Thought[/i] members tell you how bad cameras but they don’t know how the cameras are being used, they just say is bad because of privacy reasons. One member says they love the freedom of speech but at the same time I don’t see the government censoring their citizenships, maybe their newspaper but nothing more am I missing something? I heard they have immigration problem so why not show more articles showing the effects of the safety bill. Are they discriminate more by taking away their privacy than the Nation’s citizens? Do the immigrants have the same freedom as the Nation? These are questions they sort of tell but just not the amount where the players really ask themselves if freedom does have a cost or that if security has its perk for saving citizens, where is the line on that. This game deserves a 7/10! Recommend for a good short time experience for a fan of dystopian settings.

review_text_raw:
Fantastic game, I can't praise it enough. Solid story, solid characters and character progression, appealing art style, and perfect general pacing. The soundtrack, works perfectly for it- being that it's essentially a solid, subtle repeat throughout the entire game really makes those times where it picks up stand out and feel that much more important.  I really, really hope to see more from this company. And, admittedly, would love it if this premise is revisited in some way. This is the best game I've played in a long, long time. Exactly what I've been looking for. I just couldn't stop playing. I'm kind of sad that I've completely finished it. 

Issues; 
Some of the dialogue becomes a bit broken depending on your choices. Oftentimes Symes and Delacroix mentioned information that I'd intentionally not given them, later on in the story. This only really becomes noticeable on replay-but it could be worked on. Nothing like this will ever be perfect--I'm never going to seriously complain about a choice game having little issues like this. There's just too much that would have to go into a game with so many variants it to make it possible. 
There were a few lingering spelling/grammatical errors, which, given the nature of the game (Internet, instant messaging/texting), didn't really bother me all that much. (Such as Harrison tried to "fell" instead of flee.) I see these things on real articles, it's no different.
There are some bugs present, but, they're clearly being revised and, honestly, aren't game-breaking at this point.

My personal ideas; I believe there could be a little work done on the pacing of the listener- real-time DOES make it all that much more immersive, but, when it comes to replayabilty, and just the general idea of it most likely having an adult player-base, who may only have an hour or so to play before going back to their day-to-day, I feel like there should be...maybe an additional option in the settings to modify speed or..something? It's easier, and more fulfilling to put a game down for a session if you feel you were able to hit a certain level of 'achievement.' You know, the pleasure centers of the brain and all. Maybe if it were simply a more fluid letter-by-letter or syllabalic instead of by completion of a word? I don't know. 
The only other thing I could possibly suggest, would be for, if ever this title is revisited or turned into a 'series' of sorts, that it be a little more flexible? The ability to freely investigate more than is necessary--even additional people. Perhaps just in a casual sense aside from the story, since there is a necessary feeling of a 'time pinch' in the game itself. I think a lot of the audience are people like me who just like to dig, so the chance to just..index on a larger scale would be quite entertaining. 
And, lastly, the ability to generate more datachunks? This could be messy territory, though. I think this would fall into the 'would require too much forethought to ever be possible' category, but it's an idea nontheless. The system is automated, clearly, but, the evaluator should have an option to deem other things appropriate for investigation. I know there were a few things that I would have loved to have flagged that just weren't an option.

My apologies, I'm just VERY excited and passionate about this title. Guys, play it!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
There really should be a "maybe" option for steam reviews... Orwell is a decent game, just not the kind of game that is engaging for me.

Orwell is more a graphic adventure game rather than the espionage game it was advertised as. If you like Life is Strange, you'd probably like Orwell. 
Sadly this is not my cup of tea. I want to actually think and *play* a game. If I want a story I'd watch a movie or a let's play... The story had to be deeper than this for me to be interested.

The good:
Orwell did a good job at designing the user interface. It's beautiful, functional, and believable. The artstyle is unique and pleasing to the eye.
You'd find that despite the handholding, you will have to make choices that will have separate story outcomes. Some choices are more "right" than others, There're be hints in the game to help you make the right choice, so the choices are at least not just random.

The bad:
However, just like the other reviewers had pointed out, the articles and character profiles are too simplistic, it doesn't feel "real" enough. This design choice is understandable since adding fluff and pointless information just for the sake of making the sites "real" doesn't help with immersion either. What would help with immersion is the compelling content; which I find sadly lacking here... I find myself just skimming through for highlights. It's too much hand-holding for my taste. Really, they could have made it so much better by just making the relevant text unhighlighted so we have to actually spend effort reading and playing the game as "intended".

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I don't ever write reviews, but I have an overwhelming urge to say what's on my mind. With no one to rant to, I'll just use this as an outlet (and it'll provide good reference material when i come back in a couple years to figure out why i didn't like this game).

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[b]Gameplay / Mechanics[/b]

the game is simple. you parse information for the important bits and then drag and drop that information into people's profiles. the game pre-selects certain segments of text and highlights them for you and then gives you the choice of determining whether it's important or true enough to include in their file. and therein lies the problem. you're given almost no autonomy, making the game less engaging. 99% of the time, you just scroll through articles and web pages looking for the highlighted text and then dragging and dropping it. there's no limit to how much data i can gather, so i don't have to think about whether this information is important enough to include and just include it anyway. and any false information that might be misleading is made extremely obvious. like when someone lists their address as "the interwebs". if there's any data that conflicts with another piece of data, it's highlighted in yellow and presented to you as a choice. you can only choose one of these to include in their file and your decision will effect the outcome (or so i assume, having not played the game more than once). these are the more engaging parts of the game as it forces me to analyze both data chunks' context and make a real decision. but each of these moments are fleeting and within a handful of seconds, i'm back to mindlessly scrolling through files again. there's one moment in the game that breaks this trend. they limit the amount of information you can include and that was the best part of the game. i actually had to sit down and read everything before figuring out what parts i thought were important. for the first time, i actually felt immersed in this world and my role in it. that's how i think the whole game should have been. instead, i was given brainless and mundane tasks, leaving me twiddling my thumbs for the majority of the game.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[b]Story[/b]

the story is actually pretty good. the mystery is slowly unraveled as you discover more information and you're given a few twists and turns to keep you on your toes. the story is paced well, nothing feels rushed or pedantically slow and takes its own time to develop its characters and world. the characters feel real. a couple fall to mere caricatures, but the game does well at representing these characters in more than one dimension. take for example nina, a character who at first seems like an extremist but is slowly revealed to be a single mother just trying to make ends meet by doing odd jobs. the only character that irritated me was your supervisor. every time you select a piece of information, he [i]has to[/i] comment on it in some way. he either made comments that don't matter and just made me roll my eyes (like when one character said they didn't like the government and your supervisor [i]just had to say[/i] "we don't like you either"). or he recapped [i]exactly[/i] what that data chunk said. or he told you something that was already extremely obvious (like when you find out that goldfels is already dead, he says "that means he couldn't be behind the bombings and someone is impersonating him". no duh). so when he gets targeted, i don't feel a whole lot of sympathy for him. 

i do not, however, like how the story is presented. the game consciously trades its gameplay for its narrative. you start to feel like less of an investigator trying to solve a mystery and more like a disneyland park goer on the [i]it's a a small world[/i] ride. you take a backseat and just watch what happens. contrast this to [i]Firewatch[/i], a similarly narrative driven game. it's mechanics are also extremely basic and boils down to a walking simulator game, but it delivers its story masterfully and makes you feel like [i]you[/i] are uncovering everything instead of everything being spat at you (like orwell does).

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[b]Main Message[/b]

the game's main focus is to postulate the question, "should you trade privacy for security?" to which it answers "no". you take the role of what is essentially the thought police from george orwell's [i]1984[/i] and the game attempts to show you the inherent flaw of this. the end of the game breaks the fourth wall and speaks to you directly, asking you if what you've been doing is really okay. if spying on people is ethical or not, then puts the power in your hands. you can either expose the people you've been spying on this whole time or expose your boss. the problem is, the game never once makes me feel guilty or wrong or disgusted for having spied on these people's lives. in fact, it actively makes us feel justified for it. i stopped a bomb from going off in the biggest mall in the city. and when it came time to make that big decision in the end, of course i chose to expose this "thought" group because they rigged bombs and killed innocents. the game never addresses the morality of all of this and never makes me feel like i've overstepped my boundaries and question my actions. 

imagine this, as i'm going through a suspect's files (bob), i stumble upon bank statements that shows regular large-sum withdrawals. in some private conversations with his wife, he mentions having to take business trips, but his company's official records never mention any. we discover that he has a second phone with which he only contacts one person. the whole thing seems really shady and we have text messages of them planning to meet at the plaza an hour before the explosion, mentioning that he'll bring "the money". we get word that there's going to be another bombing within the hour. with the pressure mounting, we send in the police to intervene in the bob's next meeting and arrest them. during the interrogation, the bomb goes off. we find out that the bob's relation to his "contact" is a woman with which he had a one night fling and together had a baby, despite already having a family. they've been meeting together secretly so he can act as a stand-in father and support the them financially. bob loves his wife and kids and recognizes that he made a big mistake and is just trying to do his best in this crazy world. he has a responsibility to both his wife and his "contact". then sometime later (perhaps a couple chapters) we read a news article that says bob killed himself, detailing the events of his affair and how his wife divorced him. imagine how gut-wrenching that would be. to know that we ruined a guy's life because of what we did. by the end of the game, when we're asked whether or not what we did was right, that thought would would weigh heavy on my mind.

the game ends with an exposition based on your choices. in my case, the thought group is arrested and orwell is seeing full funding and support. it then has us start a profile on our own character like we've been doing all game, showing that we're also being spied on without our notice. i feel like this was supposed to be a punch to the gut, an immediate eye-opener, but it didn't do much for me. it would've been a lot more effective if it could pull information from my OS or my steam account and fill in the blanks with my real name, date of birth, email, etc. that would feel creepy and make my skin crawl a bit.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[b]Conclusion[/b]

Orwell was a missed opportunity. it had a lot of potential to address contemporary issues with the ever-real presence of a "big brother" type figure spying on us even now. but the game falls flat and fails to gain my sympathy. the game feels like it was written by a 16 year old who just read [i]1984[/i] and circle-jerks how "deep" it is.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I just finished this game. I like many of the latest reviews received this as part of a humble bundle. Unlike many of the reviewers I am no stranger to the concept of interactive fiction. As such I cannot say "WOW so unique." This game has many elements I found fascinating, and indeed I played through the whole thing in one go, a very do-able task. I think there are many things that would make me recommend it, but there are two glaring holes that I think bring it just shy of a general recommendation. I can say this, If you have never played an interactive fiction game, and the plot sounds intriguing, buy it. It is worth ten dollars. If you got it in a humble bundle or something similar, play it. You will have an entertaining few hours. If you do not fall in to either of those two camps I would recommend a pass. 

The good - 
Plot- Everything to do with the plot is great. The characters are interesting, and they do to some degree develop. The world feels complete and well rounded, The plot is where this game shines, as it should be as interactive fiction lives and dies by the plot. 
The interface - For the most part is pretty solid. There are few idiosyncrasies. The one glaring hole is the need for a few hot-keys, if only Enter and ESC, would make this much easier on the wrists, but it is as a whole soundly usable. 

The bad - For the bad I will go in to detail as to hopefully explain my point of view fully to the Devs.  There is at least one more season planned, and I would love to play it. Perhaps the Devs will hear this feedback and consider it. Before I continue though, if you have already thought “I kinda want to play this game,” do it and forget the ramblings of an old gamer. 

Choice - If the plot is what an interactive fiction game lives and dies by then choice (or for that matter the illusion of choice) is what allows it to breath. In Orwell the idea of choice dies very quickly, and never returns. There are several pivotal moments which finds the player, through the narrative, put in a position to make a pivotal choice. All the relevant characters are obviously pointing at you and saying you decide. I never really felt like there was any choices to be made. Either The player is not given enough context to understand the consequences of that choice, in these cases you are just blindly choosing one of two options and made to accept the consequences. Or you cannot progress until you make the choice. 

At the heart of this, in my opinion, is the engine for which you as the player progress through the narrative. You are told at the very beginning of the game that you cannot progress until you have uploaded certain information. Which pieces of information allows for progression is up to the game. The premise of games like this in which it is up to the player to provide or not provide information to the antagonist is a great juxtaposition to make the player feel invested, and in many cases responsible for the consequences levied on the characters in the narrative. Games like “Papers Please” and “Beholder” levy this mechanic very well. In Orwell you cannot progress without giving the Antagonist certain information. This kills the illusion of choice, and make the rest of the narrative lose it's bite. Because I cannot NOT provide certain information the consequences are not my fault. The game made me do it. Especially in those moments where you have several data points you can give, and you need to choose between them, but if you choose wrong the game does not go forward, you end up throwing whatever data points at the wall, even those bits of data you do not want to provide, in order to get the game to continue. 

I realize why it was written this way. You cannot write a narrative which has ALL possibilities. So in order to move forward you need the player to trip certain triggers. An elegant way around this in my opinion would be to allow the information to be presented in "real time." This allows the narrative to continue while allowing the player more of a choice in the way it unfolds. I think this would greatly improve the impact of the game. 

The Twist - (mild spoiler warning) 
If you have read this far then I doubt this will really be a spoiler, but just in case, you have been warned.


There is a twist at the end. All good who-done-it's have them. This is no exception. My issue with the twist at the end of Orwell dove tails in to the idea of choice. There is no way you the player, let alone the character you play in the game, could predict it. There are no data points that I found that will allow you to discover the twist in game. Therefore it feels arbitrary. Once again the narrative loses impact because it does not feel like the player could intercede. The game is going to do what it is going to do and you are just pulled along to see what happens. that is what novels, TV shows, movies, and comic books are for. In fact I could see this story being a great Rashamon-Style comic, but as an interactive fiction I think this game falls flat. 

Summery - In summation I think if you are interested in games as an art form, or are just curios about what happens in this particular narrative, then this is worth while. I look forward to see if any of these issues are fixed in the next chapter. I do not regret my time "playing" this game. but I think in the end, The impact of the events was greatly blunted by the mechanics with which the narrative is presented. That seems a shame to me as the story could be quit impact-full if only the illusion of choice was maintained through out. In a narrative the promise of the premise is key, 
"Only the information you provide will be seen by the security forces and acted upon. You decide what gets seen and what does not, influencing how the suspects will be perceived." 
and this narrative missed that promise.
review_text_clean: I just finished this game. I like many of the latest reviews received this as part of a humble bundle. Unlike many of the reviewers I am no stranger to the concept of interactive fiction. As such I cannot say "WOW so unique." This game has many elements I found fascinating, and indeed I played through the whole thing in one go, a very do-able task. I think there are many things that would make me recommend it, but there are two glaring holes that I think bring it just shy of a general recommendation. I can say this, If you have never played an interactive fiction game, and the plot sounds intriguing, buy it. It is worth ten dollars. If you got it in a humble bundle or something similar, play it. You will have an entertaining few hours. If you do not fall in to either of those two camps I would recommend a pass. The good - Plot- Everything to do with the plot is great. The characters are interesting, and they do to some degree develop. The world feels complete and well rounded, The plot is where this game shines, as it should be as interactive fiction lives and dies by the plot. The interface - For the most part is pretty solid. There are few idiosyncrasies. The one glaring hole is the need for a few hot-keys, if only Enter and ESC, would make this much easier on the wrists, but it is as a whole soundly usable. The bad - For the bad I will go in to detail as to hopefully explain my point of view fully to the Devs. There is at least one more season planned, and I would love to play it. Perhaps the Devs will hear this feedback and consider it. Before I continue though, if you have already thought “I kinda want to play this game,” do it and forget the ramblings of an old gamer. Choice - If the plot is what an interactive fiction game lives and dies by then choice (or for that matter the illusion of choice) is what allows it to breath. In Orwell the idea of choice dies very quickly, and never returns. There are several pivotal moments which finds the player, through the narrative, put in a position to make a pivotal choice. All the relevant characters are obviously pointing at you and saying you decide. I never really felt like there was any choices to be made. Either The player is not given enough context to understand the consequences of that choice, in these cases you are just blindly choosing one of two options and made to accept the consequences. Or you cannot progress until you make the choice. At the heart of this, in my opinion, is the engine for which you as the player progress through the narrative. You are told at the very beginning of the game that you cannot progress until you have uploaded certain information. Which pieces of information allows for progression is up to the game. The premise of games like this in which it is up to the player to provide or not provide information to the antagonist is a great juxtaposition to make the player feel invested, and in many cases responsible for the consequences levied on the characters in the narrative. Games like “Papers Please” and “Beholder” levy this mechanic very well. In Orwell you cannot progress without giving the Antagonist certain information. This kills the illusion of choice, and make the rest of the narrative lose it's bite. Because I cannot NOT provide certain information the consequences are not my fault. The game made me do it. Especially in those moments where you have several data points you can give, and you need to choose between them, but if you choose wrong the game does not go forward, you end up throwing whatever data points at the wall, even those bits of data you do not want to provide, in order to get the game to continue. I realize why it was written this way. You cannot write a narrative which has ALL possibilities. So in order to move forward you need the player to trip certain triggers. An elegant way around this in my opinion would be to allow the information to be presented in "real time." This allows the narrative to continue while allowing the player more of a choice in the way it unfolds. I think this would greatly improve the impact of the game. The Twist - (mild spoiler warning) If you have read this far then I doubt this will really be a spoiler, but just in case, you have been warned. There is a twist at the end. All good who-done-it's have them. This is no exception. My issue with the twist at the end of Orwell dove tails in to the idea of choice. There is no way you the player, let alone the character you play in the game, could predict it. There are no data points that I found that will allow you to discover the twist in game. Therefore it feels arbitrary. Once again the narrative loses impact because it does not feel like the player could intercede. The game is going to do what it is going to do and you are just pulled along to see what happens. that is what novels, TV shows, movies, and comic books are for. In fact I could see this story being a great Rashamon-Style comic, but as an interactive fiction I think this game falls flat. Summery - In summation I think if you are interested in games as an art form, or are just curios about what happens in this particular narrative, then this is worth while. I look forward to see if any of these issues are fixed in the next chapter. I do not regret my time "playing" this game. but I think in the end, The impact of the events was greatly blunted by the mechanics with which the narrative is presented. That seems a shame to me as the story could be quit impact-full if only the illusion of choice was maintained through out. In a narrative the promise of the premise is key, "Only the information you provide will be seen by the security forces and acted upon. You decide what gets seen and what does not, influencing how the suspects will be perceived." and this narrative missed that promise.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I am really conflicted on this game.
On one hand, it looks and sounds excellent, being extremely stylish and immersing the player into a dystopian world of total surveillence, the characters being (mostly) well-written and felt alive. All the websites, social networks, advertisement banners and the online banter is very realistic, they even included some made-up memes for their made-up world that looked like something that could actually exist in ours. Also, had a high-quality localisation to my native language (Russian) and i didn't really feel like i was missing anything out by not playing it in its original language.

Now, on the other hand. This game mostly play out like a visual novel, where you make your choices in whether or not to upload a certain bit of marked information into the system. There are also bits with "conflicting facts" in which you also can make a choice that can affect how will the story develop. And, for the most of the game, yor choices do matter: will a certain character go to jail or manage to escape the police? Will you frame someone who made a minor break of the law into something more incriminating, so he will actually get arrested? It is incredubly nice: as a player, you feel the real power of someone with the tools for total surveillence, with only your own morals that might prevent you from abusing that power. 
The story itself plays out nicely, keeping the player in suspence, with enough of "Oh god" moments to keep you invested... right until its final part. For me, it really felt like the game did a U-turn and started pushing its morals on me, instead of letting me, as a player, to make the final choice. Sure, there are multiple endings, but all of them mostly convey the same idea (no spoilers), which, i felt, was insulting to all the choices i made before it. I expected it to be more "morally-grey", especially considering how well it started, but in the end it tried to be a lesson in how you should think. And those very same people tell us about thought crimes? Ironic.

Not recommended, unless you are fine with the game's morale.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[i] *very, very minor spoilers are hidden* [/i]

[h1] TL;DR "The Last Enemy" without Cucumberpatch [/h1]

Admittedly, the above reference might skate over a few people's heads, but the core themes are the same. Based loosely around the old US Total Information Awareness system, the game explores the issues around predictive profiling and human bias.

The details are what makes this game shine: The irrelevant online junk, the typos and slang, the shoddy dating websites, even the pages load like a real browser. The user interface is slick and easy to use. For that extra immersion, I really recommend taking your time to read as much as you can. It's not as quirky as DX:HR, but it's close.

The characters are wonderfully complex, if occasionally stereotypical. I love the "show, don't tell" approach of implying their personalities through online interactions, and the format of the game is really unique -- I've never played a game quite like this before.

My biggest gripe is gameplay. There is none. Everything is highlighted and every conflict displayed, which underwhelms the idea that [spoiler] your bias invalidates Orwell [/spoiler], and eventually turns the game into a mindless point-and-click. There are no difficult puzzles or decisions beyond moral ones, and even those seem to have little bearing on the outcome. The ending certainly felt a little shoehorned, and the [spoiler] twist a little out of character [/spoiler]. It's best to view this game as an interactive story rather than a game. I'd have also liked the ability to replay individual episodes - restarting the game just to change a single decision in ep. 5 is a little inconvenient.

As a very fast reader, the entire game took 3-4 hours to complete, bearing in mind I read absolutely everything. Half the time seems to be spent on watching conversations scroll in real time, which is realistic, but not for the impatient. If you don't like reading or text-based games, don't bother.

I really do recommend this game. The tense, compelling plot had me eagerly waiting for the next episode. You do become emotionally involved with the characters, even with a week between episodes. A little shallow at times, but enjoyable nonetheless.

11/10 would hack the local fishing society again.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] How far are you willing to go to protect the populace? [/h1]

[i]Orwell[/i] is a “visual novel” style game in which you have the ability to follow cyber-breadcrumbs in order to slowly uncover suspect’s online lives. Your goal? Stop a terrorist organization (?) from bombing public spaces. Your tools? As an agent, you are privy to the entirety of your target’s posts, articles, phone calls, emails, etc. Use this information to reveal more and more relevant webpages and conversations. The catch? You’re overlooked by a supervisor and you must choose what information to upload. This supervisor can only see the bits of information you feed him, so choose wisely or risk ruining an innocent’s life. The challenge? Upload only enough information to gain new leads, but not jump to conclusions. 

Are you really helping the greater good by invading the privacy of the few? Or have you caused more harm than good, muddling in affairs you should have never been in? Are the internet spies of today, really the superheroes of tomorrow? Find out by stepping into these large, cyber shoes. Act quickly and stop a harmful event in its tracks, or wait it out and discover it was a false alarm. Big brother is watching you. You are watching the people. Lives are on the line. Decide. 

Then watch as you say, [b]“I never meant for this to happen.”[/b]

Let me start off this review by saying I’m one who really enjoys a story-based game. I particularly enjoy consequence based story games (like [i]Telltale[/i]). If that’s not your cup of tea, this game is not for you. If you’re still interested, here’s the pros and cons for the game so far.

[h1]Pros:[/h1] [b]Interesting social commentary.[/b] There’s no denying that this is the age of technology, and with that comes a whole new slew of problems that our forefathers never could have foresaw when drafting the constitution. [i]Orwell[/i] heavily and obviously alludes to the current hot topics of freedom of internet access, government access to our personal files and correspondences, and general cyber security we see crop up in the news time and time again. 

[b]Easy interface.[/b] There’s not much to learn but drag and drop. Your un-uploaded data chunks are marked so you don’t lose track of what you’ve read, need to read, and are saving for later.

[b]More unique game flow.[/b] Events don’t happen unless you upload data chucks, leaving you to explore the branches of plot in whatever order feels natural to you. It does still feel a bit restricted, though, (see “A bit linear, limited” in cons) a perhaps more of a pseudo-free-directional choice. (But isn’t the concept of freedom what this game is all about?) 

[b]Intriguing artwork.[/b] The geometric artistic style lends itself to unconsciously nod its head towards the cyber-oriented world of the game. It ties in beautifully to the theme of the game—from the logo to the interface—without being too aggressive.

[h1]Cons:[/h1] [strike][b]A better save system!![/b][/strike] Update has added a rewind system, but I have not played since [strike]I cannot stress this enough. Since this is a consequence-based game, I’d like to be able to start from the end episode one, or so, with my decisions staying the same, and only make changes to my decisions from there out, with my profiles branching out from my first play through plot line. Starting over from the beginning is too much of a grind. Even a way to speed up messaging/call text on the second (and beyond) playthrough would be better for acheivement hunters or people just curious about the other endings. Examples of games with a good save system for this style of gameplay include [i]A Wolf Among Us[/i] and [i]Papers, Please.[/i][/strike]

[b]A bit linear, limited.[/b] There were some moments I wish some bit of text was highlighted (you may only drag and upload highlighted data chunks) since I wanted to explore that avenue of inquiry, but [i]Orwell[/i] had other plans. This gave the game a restricted feeling. It does not leave the game open to a world of naturally-occurring red herrings (only game-constructed ones, not user constructed), which I think would have added much more depth to the game. Also, it’s glaringly obvious which pieces of text carry great significance. (Those will be the ones with conflicting evidence) so sometimes the challenge of deciding to report information right away or wait was quite discernible, offering no challenge. Although, I will say that there are a few nuggets of data I uploaded without believing they would have as large of a consequence as they did. 

[b]Short.[/b] There’s only a little over forty minutes of game play per episode, and with five episodes, this leads to roughly four hours of gameplay (assuming you don’t replay events). I follow a rule of thumb of at least $1 to 1 hour of gameplay, so in that regard, it’s a bit pricey. Just wait for a sale. 

[h1]Remark:[/h1] [b]Play in one sitting[/b] (or as close to that as possible, if you don't have a full 4-5 hours to dedicate to one game) The flow and length of the game lends itself to be optimally played in one sitting. Taking a break and not have a comprehensive refresher (like the cinematic playbacks of key choices in [i]Telltale[/i] games) of your choices and actions is jarring to the enjoyment of the storyline in my opinion.

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
[b]I’d recommend buying [i]Orwell[/i] when on sale.[/b] It has an interesting and captivating storyline, despite some need of polishing. The interface, flow, and artwork lend itself to be an immersive experience into the lives of the people you are spying on to protect. Also, the current social commentary gives a real-world depth to the game. It does feel a bit restricting at times, and the story is short. The save system leaves much to be desired, since I would like to more easily explore all possibilities of my choices. But, despite these factors it was still enjoyable and fun to play.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Game Summary: [/h1] 
This game doesn't fit into most normal game conventions and acts more like a cautionary tale.  By allowing the gamer to take the seat of a possible government agent in a program giving you so much power and access over people's lives, it lets you determine what you take away from it.  Is it a necessary evil for the government to have this much depth and access to what people are posting online, downloaded on their various devices, and talking about in their phone calls?  Or is that question alone already pushing too far, as people have an inherent right to privacy?  Wisely the game developer merely posits this to its audience, instead of preaching what is or isn't appropriate behavior in the 21st Century and beyond.  


[h1] Pros: [/h1] 
•	The first playthrough where I was intruding so far into people's lives made me feel uncomfortable.  Not scared or tense, just somewhat uncomfortable.  I think it's because invading people's privacy to this extent, knowing how easily the same thing could happen to you, is rather unsettling.  Medical records and mental health histories, various profiles and online communities you participate in (theoretically behind an alias), personal conversations and chats, all available for someone to read through.  For someone to comb through for any signs of instability, derangement, or evidence that this person isn't a law-abiding citizen, but a dirty crook.  This is dangerously close to criminalizing people for wrong-think.  
•	This game shines in its story and writing, because the characters feel real.  Their various profiles and conversations, how they become both paranoid and angry, but still only guessing at how bad things already are regarding the government's intrusion into their lives.  It gives the game a greater sense of reality and immersion, which is key.  They may not be rocket scientists, but they do take steps to avoid being screwed over, though if you're being a good big brother, it's already too late for them.  
•	I love that what I choose to upload can have a pretty big impact on how what the characters are saying and doing is interpreted.  It can either be seen as the acts of an innocent person, or the pattern of someone who's a low-down crook.  It raises the question of how any of us would look from the outside to someone who'd see all of our online activity.
•	The music acts as ambient background.  It's very low-key, and could theoretically be the sort of soft tune a government office would play to keep employees from getting too antsy.  This is for the most part, but when the climax of each day/act builds, then it picks up and gets you on edge.


[h1] Cons: [/h1] 
• 	Though it would take more time in both development and gameplay, it'd be nice if there were more people for you to look into who turned out to be red herrings. game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Wow I am more than impressed with this game. I am a big fan of the game genre of "Papers, Please", "This is the police" and similar games. I think when games explore your morals and hits you right in your cognitive dissonance. This game does this incredibly well. Surveilence is a difficult subject. There are pros and cons that vary between people.

This game sets your objective as having you aid in finding the suspect for a terrorist attack. This is of course a justifiable action and is in good favor for the public. You quickly start having conflicting thoughts about whether the people you're spying on and the information you gather is relevant at all. I am the type of person who is really interested in other people's affairs. This game absolutely worked wonders on this quirk of mine because I found it difficult to resist to look deeper in people's personal lives. I bet you will too constantly convince yourself that "this guy's past relationship drama might prove useful later".

The writing in this game is absolutely amazing in my honest opinion. This game felt real. The information layout, news articles, blogs, emails, texts, calls all felt real. The way you quickly progress from getting basic information on one person such as their name and occupation suddenly turns into having direct sneaky access to their desktop files, bank account activity and search history. You will find a lot of surprises in this game and lots of VERY difficult choices. There is a lot of conflicting ideas this game forces on you. For example you are presented with 2 or 3 very contradicting pieces of information. Sometimes it is easy to choose based on the source of where this info came from but when the consequences are severe, you are under pressure to make the right choice as there is no going back.

One downfall of this game is that there are some slight errors in the scripting that messes up the flow. For example there are certain bits which I suppose are meant to be discovered in a certain sequence but its possible to do it in the wrong sequence, resulting in dialogue that doesn't fit in. Alerting the higher ups of a threat after it already happened results in them thanking you for the useful information and that they will be prepared...even though this happened just recently and they were not prepared. The game also decides on itself which information is relevant or not and kind of makes you feel bad for collecting everything you might feel is necessary but thankfully you are not outright punished for it. Another big error I noticed was with relationships. I find out that a character has been married in the past and add it to the database but the database instead labels the character as currently married which is considered as wrong information until you find out more details later.

All in all these negatives do not affect the game much. This game is worth full price and I think is a must buy with a discount.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Pros:
- Art style is interesting and engaging
- Story is well crafted and immersive
- Exposition isn't forced on you, but it is there if you wish to learn more about the world or certain characters
- Creators clearly spent a lot of time and effort on the setting 
- The game tackles some pretty engaging ethical dilemas that are applicable to the world we live in

Cons:
- Click and drag simulator 2016
- Uninspired gameplay mechanics 
- Constant handholding (I kept thinking I was in a long tutorial but that's just how the game is)
- Very binary choices (he did it vs she did it/ she did the right thing vs she is bad)
- No real detective work the game just tells you everything
- The game treats you like an idiot by having a sidekick tell you what each piece of info means


Other things that bothered me:

-      Chat/phone calls move too fast to keep up with uploading the 'chunks' that appear and you're forced to either ignore the dialogue progression and try to click on a certain chuck as the screen constantly shifts or wait until the exchange is  done to upload anything (or maybe I was just too slow).

-      Music shifts in tone dramtically whenever 'shocking info' is revealed which makes the game feel very linear (which it is) instead of just letting you stumble upon the info yourself and make your own conclusions as to what is important. The music changes give the feeling of "This was a scripted event that I experienced at a designated time."

-      Your partner/boss just tells you things so you don't really have to do any investigation yourself which is kind the whole point of the game. 

-      You are fed information in a pretty constant chronological stream instead being given all the info at once and having to sort through it with your brain. The game treats you like a baby and doesn't give you your next treat until you click and drag the things on the page it just gave you. 

-      The game established this rhythm really early of scrolling through a page, clicking on stuff, listening to your buddy pal guy tell you stuff, being given a new page, then repeating.

-      The fact that the chats/calls don't start until you actively bring them up is quite harmful to immersion (why would the people wait to start talking on the phone for 5 seconds until I'm monitoring them? Just have them act like normal humans and not wait for the player).

-      The gameplay would be a lot better if the events driving the characters weren't so close to the present. If we as players were given this new technology to help solve a crime in the past (several months at least) it would eliminate the need to have these awfully convenient text conversations and phone calls every 5 seconds that always have important info. What I'm saying is put the event in the past so that the player can be given a bunch of call transcripts and chat logs to sift through instead of being handed the info.

-      The very nature of how the game highlights all of the important info for you makes you question what your job really is and why anyone would need you to do it. If they already have a system that determines what is important and human operators who interpret the data (your boss/partner guy), why the hell do they need you???

-      The info highlighting eventually has you just scrolling through pages until something lights up or you get an update instead of actually reading the page and deciding what is important and what is irrelevant.




This is not a bad game by any means. It's just always frustrating when I see one of these "choices matter" games where there's clearly a certain path you're encouraged to take and you really aren't free to do things your own way.

While I had pretty high expectations for this game after coming off a Hacknet binge, I just feel as though the game is trying to pretend to be something it's not. Just market the game for what it is, a linear narrative experience.

I'm very aware that since I did not finish the game my perspective is limited to what I played, but what I played I did not enjoy, so I cannot reccomend this game.

TL;DR: This game is a very and hand-holdy linear story based experience while it is advertised to be a sort of detective

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What a wasted opportunity.

I went into this game wanting to like it - I really did. To be clear - I played through the entire game, finishing each of the 5 chapters.

Orwell is ostensibly a game about a surveillance state gone terribly wrong - but almost at every opportunity, it fails to make any meaningful point and constantly gets in its own way.

It starts bad. Rather than giving you, as a player, the agency to incriminate and potentially ruin the lives of the people you are surveilling, the game immediately puts you at arms-length. You are nothing more than a data collector with the ability to find and store information, but not make any meaningful analysis or conclusions about this data. Worse, it pairs you with the clumsily-written and drearily heavy-handed Symes - the *actual* investigator, who acts on the information you upload and is a constant source of awkward, immersion-breaking, and stupid commentary. 

It's true that, in principle, the data you choose to upload can affect the lives and outcomes of the people whose privacy you're invading - the trouble is that there's no real incentive to do so. Oftentimes, you must upload certain pieces of data in order to move the story along - which makes sense, because you're nothing more than a glorified data monkey clicking blue text and throwing it into a database. If you choose to hide a piece of information, it's not clear whether or not you'll be able to progress through the story. If you get something wrong (in the extremely limited range of things you are even allowed to get wrong), there are few consequences - an issue exacerbated by how distanced you are from everything that goes down. You don't really get to make the call, figure out the deduction, or even choose whether or not you should be wielding the awesome power you do. You either progress the story, or you don't - Symes is the one who gets to actually decide.

What's worse is that each of the characters in the game are utterly unlikable - the crimes you investigate them for are legitimate crimes that hurt real innocents and pose genuine dangers to the society in which they inhabit - the moral quandary that this game should so naturally lend itself to (the invasion of privacy, the loss of intimacy, that everybody is a criminal under mass surveillance, etc.,) is utterly and absolutely wasted. Instead, you are railroaded through a specific set of documents, webpages, and chats (not giving you any opportunity to actually deduce anything) in which not one of the horribly written characters manages to endear themselves.

Ultimately, this game is trying to tell you two stories - a by the numbers B-grade mystery plot filled with unlikable and annoying characters, and a study of the evolution of mass surveillance in an increasingly tech-focussed society. In so doing, they tell neither one well. They did an incredible disservice to a barely-interesting character study of modern revolutionaries, and an even greater disservice to the core (and seemingly obvious!) issues with state-driven, indiscriminate surveillance.

Let's not even start with the UI. What begins as a somewhat interesting ability to listen in on conversations quickly becomes a tiresome and arduous chore - there are a couple of moments in which listening in on a conversation live makes sense, but these moments are few and far between. For the most part, you are treated to a disastrously slow chat message filled with stilted dialogue and unfortunate Fellow Kids idioms, or an equally slow voice transcription. I quickly began to dread these moments, rather than feel the rush of uncovering a potential clue.

At no point do you feel like a data wizard, an unscrupulous detective, or even a curious and detached researcher. You just feel bored. 

Orwell is, despite its polished presentation, a total and undeniable bust. 

Desperately trying to cram all of the social commentary it should have been exploring over the entire game into its final chapter, it fails to make a meaningful statement about mass surveillance and the police state. 

Having written shallow, stupid, stereotypical characters with zero likable traits or humanizing aspects (each of whom are also genuine suspects in an act of actual terrorism) it fails to present a compelling character study of the 21st-century revolutionary.

By railroading you during every part of the core gameplay loop and anchoring you at the waist with a bumbling, intrusive character (who gets to make *all* the calls and draw all the *actual* conclusions), they fail to provide a satisfying, thrilling, or even baseline interesting detective experience.

Finally, by forgetting the most fundamental principles in their clunky, limited, and careless design, they failed to provide an even halfway tolerable interface. 

I didn't even get to enjoy interacting with the game.

Orwell is a disaster. You will get nothing from it, no insight, no emotion, no deductions, and no surprises. It wastes every bit of the opportunity it had to say something meaningful.

This is my Two Minutes Hate - and Orwell deserves every second of it.

Ultimately, this game is trying to tell you two stories - a by the numbers B-grade mystery plot filled with unlikable and annoying characters, and a study of the evolution of mass surveillance in an increasingly tech-focussed society. In so doing, they tell neither one well. They did an incredible disservice to a barely-interesting character study of modern revolutionaries, and an even greater disservice to the core (and seemingly obvious!) issues with state-driven, indiscriminate surveillance. Let's not even start with the UI. What begins as a somewhat interesting ability to listen in on conversations quickly becomes a tiresome and arduous chore - there are a couple of moments in which listening in on a conversation live makes sense, but these moments are few and far between. For the most part, you are treated to a disastrously slow chat message filled with stilted dialogue and unfortunate Fellow Kids idioms, or an equally slow voice transcription. I quickly began to dread these moments, rather than feel the rush of uncovering a potential clue. At no point do you feel like a data wizard, an unscrupulous detective, or even a curious and detached researcher. You just feel bored. Orwell is, despite its polished presentation, a total and undeniable bust. Desperately trying to cram all of the social commentary it should have been exploring over the entire game into its final chapter, it fails to make a meaningful statement about mass surveillance and the police state. Having written shallow, stupid, stereotypical characters with zero likable traits or humanizing aspects (each of whom are also genuine suspects in an act of actual terrorism) it fails to present a compelling character study of the 21st-century revolutionary. By railroading you during every part of the core gameplay loop and anchoring you at the waist with a bumbling, intrusive character (who gets to make *all* the calls and draw all the *actual* conclusions), they fail to provide a satisfying, thrilling, or even baseline interesting detective experience. Finally, by forgetting the most fundamental principles in their clunky, limited, and careless design, they failed to provide an even halfway tolerable interface. I didn't even get to enjoy interacting with the game. Orwell is a disaster. You will get nothing from it, no insight, no emotion, no deductions, and no surprises. It wastes every bit of the opportunity it had to say something meaningful. This is my Two Minutes Hate - and Orwell deserves every second of it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A good game in principle but fell short along the way.

I really wanted to like this game more.
Initially I was very intrigued, however the longer I played the more everything started to fall apart.
First off - this needs voice acting.
I don't think every line in the game needs voice acting, but at least the phone calls and the advisers should've been voiced.
Secondly - add more red herrings/alternative plot lines that a player can trip on.
This game initially seemed very vast and branched out to me, yet as I played it through and then replayed a couple more times for the achievements I realised that it is still very linear and there's not much you can do that will have a very big effect on your playthrough.
Third - there were a few plot lines in the game that were just never explained or touched on again. I think the game could've been more fleshed out if these plotlines were explored more.
Fourth - not being able to change datachunks. I understand that the whole plot is built on the idea that you cannot keep changing data, but it just felt like an artificial boundary for seemingly no reason.
Lastly - I couldn't help but feel like some of the writing for the characters was just off (it's hard to put into words but something just didn't feel right about the way the interactions went).

Overall the game was ok, but its just not something I would recommend to someone else.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game is a pretty neat take on the "actual computer as game interface" genre made famous by (the much better) Her Story, and it is a provocative take on government spying as well. The gameplay itself is fun and interesting, but not nearly as deep as it could be. Unlike in Her Story, I rarely felt like I was truly investigating; between the red highlights, the prompts from your handler, and the linear structure of the investigation itself, I more often than not felt like the game was just leading me along by the nose. Indeed, the prompts from the handler almost ruin the whole experience - in addition to giving you several totally unnecessary hints, he often comments on the investigation itself in ways that are very disruptive and eye-rolly (i.e. "wow, what a strange development!"). I'd rather just be allowed to form opinions on the narrative myself, thank you very much, but unfortunately he cannot be turned off. 

Still, it is definitely worth checking out, especially for its price point. I particularly enjoyed the social network mapping mechanic, the way that you gradually see the connections build between all the people you are investigating. Overall, the game could have been much better, but still a decent game.
