game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This is a difficult one to critique because whether or not you like it is mainly dependent on whether you like the narrative and how it is told. I’m not going to pretend that I know a huge amount about a good story well told, so when it comes to my thoughts on said story, take them with a grain of salt. Before I discuss that though, let’s talk about the game a bit.

[h1]“Interactive” Story[/h1]

In context, you are supposed to be a sort of investigator searching for clues about persons of interest via their emails, social media feeds, and phone conversations. I wouldn’t use the word “investigate” to describe the gameplay. Every import piece of information is already highlighted for you and you just need to drag-and-drop them to the appropriate location. When it comes selecting which documents you want to search through, there are indicators that tell which ones have important data-chunks. You don’t really have to read through the documents and phone texts unless you want story context.

This does streamline the gameplay experience, though. With a lot of story based adventure or point-and-click games, there is a risk of getting stuck at one part and losing all immersion in indirection proportion to mounting frustration. Orwell doesn’t have this problem as it is always very clear where you are supposed to look and this keeps a smooth pacing. As I mentioned earlier, this does contribute to the whole experience not feeling much like a traditional game as it feels much more like a guided tour of the characters and narrative progression. Perhaps a system where you have to highlight pieces of text you feel are important, and if you got the right piece then the story could progress? That may have been the original idea, but that could lead to many frustrations if you just barely missed the part of a quote you were supposed to get.

The only real gameplay in here is when there are two pieces of data that conflict with each other and you have to decide which one to submit to your superior. This could come in the form of two phone conversations by a character where one conversation makes him sound violent and the other makes him sound peaceful. Which one you submit will determine if that character gets arrested later in the story. This factors into a bit of a moral choice system regarding whether you try to paint the main characters and virtuous activists or terrorists. I feel an opportunity was missed to have more greatly divergent storylines to make the player feel like they have a real impact on the world. As it stands, your decisions only change minor events and what ending you get, with most of the heavy decision making existing in the last episode only.

[h1]Interactive “Story”[/h1]

With everything I’ve had to say about the gameplay thus far, you may be a bit perplexed as to why I recommend Orwell. Once again, this isn’t a typical [i]game[/i]. It’s a story with a bit more user control over the pace at which you progress through it. So how is the story?

Pretty good, actually.

The subject matter: government surveillance, is very topical and the game does a good job of showing the many different angles and opinions that people have about it. From those that try to peacefully discuss the issue, publicly criticize it, or are indifferent to it, every character seems believable and for the most part are consistent. The plot is revealed at a steady pace and is able to constantly engage. Appropriate music cues help to reinforce when something drastic has just taken place or when a particularly important piece of data is discovered and it does a good job of drawing you in. The last episode starts to deteriorate when the story starts to massively diverge and the amount of documents and computers to search through becomes overwhelming compared to the rest of the story.

While the data chunks are the most important piece of the story, there is a lot of text to sift through and it fleshes out the characters and game world quite well. A lot of it is unnecessary and for a while I thought that a small sub-plot about terrorism in another country was going to turn out to be a major plot device because the game kept bringing it up, but that ended up being nothing important. Also, documents and conversations are never deleted, so you are free to browse through them at your leisure and one small link could lead you down a rabbit’s hole worth of information. Having assessed these can be handy if the story calls for you to investigate those links and you’re already familiar with them, which does occasionally make you feel like a real investigator.

There are a few off moments when the characters don’t feel believable because we only see them communicate via text. Towards the end, [spoiler]everyone is panicking because they have discovered the Orwell system and can’t figure out how to deal with it,[/spoiler] and sometimes text just isn’t the best way to convey those sorts of emotions. These are hardly deal breakers though because what it boils down to is that whenever I would start the game up, it wasn’t because I felt some obligation to finish it. It was because I wanted to know what happens next. And no matter how many trivial nit-picks I have with the story, that single fact means I have to acknowledge that the story is engaging.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

Orwell is a story, and not much of a game. Whatever gameplay is present serves entirely to incrementally progress you through the story and not present any kind of and challenge by itself. An experience like this lives and dies on whether or not its story is engaging which, to me at least, it certainly was.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
In the wake of a recent bombing, someone needs to be tasked to help investigate the suspected bombers. That someone is you. You are in charge of what goes in the system and what doesn't. But is there more to it? Is there a group planning it all together, or just one person? Do you paint them as terrorists or do you leave out enough information to show them as innocent?

[h1]Welcome to Orwell[/h1]
Orwell is one of those stories that is best to go blind in, since it is the most effective the first time. Hearing or seeing anything that is related to the main story, especially the end, ruins how you would play. But why? You are playing yourself, a new recruit of a programed named Orwell tasked to investigate suspicious people regarding the recent bombing. Through, which I wished happened more, a cutscene perfectly showing why and what this game is with only visuals. If you read 1984 Orwell is similar to how the government watches their people as it was influenced from George Orwell's books.

[h1]Datachunk Uploaded[/h1]
Down to it's core, you only read highlighted items, or datachunks, and dragging them to profiles for uploading. But there is much more if you are willing. Datachunks are meant to be evaluated, is this noteworthy to put on someone's profile? Do you purposefully make someone look worse or better? Should you upload every little thing? The game tried to put you in this mindset by your supervisor's comments and by conflicting datachunks (represented by a yellow highlight) to show you can't upload every little thing. Of course, there are datachunks needed to continue. Most of the time it is very apparent the datachunk is needed as it gives something new you can look through, solve a conflicting datachunk, or a sound cue picks up. This is all combined to represent how you view the situation. How you view the people you were tasked to investigate. How you have an influence on how their life will go after Orwell injected you into their lives. Sure, they do make their own decisions, but you have the power to have them forever be seen as a threat by the government.

Your first playthrough is key. It is how you would react in this situation, not how some character would. You do not know anything except what you gather. All other playthroughs after that is to see what could have happened if you did something differently. Anything you know about the main storyline ruins how you make decisions in the game. So I do recommend knowing as little as possible to get the most out of it.

I suppose Orwell is too easy. You have a supervisor meant to guide you, not only in Orwell but to guide your progress through the main storyline. It is very easy to just scroll down till you see phrases or words highlighted. Trying to find conflicting datachunks quickly to get past. While there is nothing stopping you, Orwell does try to encourage you to read. The many articles and websites you visit build the world as you continually gain access. In a way, the people you investigate brings you into the world as you unknowingly destroy theirs each datachunk at a time. There has been arguments about taking away the automatic highlighting, as why should you be hired if they have a system that does it, but there is too much that one can assume is needed. It could easily become entering random phrases or words till you get it right. So this way of highlighting does take away this confusion of what is and isn't noteworthy in a wall of text or conversations.

[h1]Sound[/h1]
There's limited sounds to Orwell, having background music and computer sounds. The background soundtrack never really changes until something notewrothy and important comes into view. While computer sounds symbolizes actions, such as a sound of a phone for a phone call and a click as datachunks are being entered.

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
While you do stare at a screen of your computer, Orwell has an interesting style when it comes to pictures. They build people with polygons. This gives an interesting visual that pops out when surrounded by text and brightening up the screen. The opening cutscene is one of the places that does not primarily showcase this style, going for more of an shaded outline. While the visuals are minimal, it does look appealing.

[h1]Performance[/h1]
Orwell easily runs well. Only having a few seconds of loading in the beginning of each chapter to load everything. There also seems to be a rare bug, not allowing the player to drag or view the preview of the datachunk. Thankfully, the datachunk is not needed to continue with the story, as it persists through the save, so it may only bother those who view it as an important datachunk to include in a profile.

[h1]Revisiting Orwell[/h1]
As said before, Orwell thrives on the first playthrough. After that, you know what's going to happen. You know what choices affects those you were assigned to. That first playthrough may be remembered as you replay, but so everthing major to the story. This is where you should look up guides as more playthroughs are solely for achievements that were off of the course you took. There are a total of three offical endings, all having subtle changed down the road. There's not much replayability but to see the difference the decisions have on the suspects.

[h1]Report[/h1]
+ Art style
+ Convincing characters; can easily be viewed as real people
+ Compelling story

+/- Your choice to see the world of Orwell
+/- Can be seen as constantly holding your hand

- The phone calls and texts are either too slow or too fast. You have to activate the certain call/text for it to start, breaking immersion since no one will wait till you come into the picture. If you are fast enough you can get two calls or texts (or a combination of the two) at the same time since you are likely to look at something else during other playthroughs. 

Orwell is one of those must play games. With the close hitting theme that may soon become reality. With all chapters released, you can easily have 2-3 hours of gamethrough per playthrough depending on how you choose to play. Orwell shows that you are being watched in some ways, even now, and that even you won't have the best interest for others if they have the possibility to be threats to society. Do not be afraid of going into Orwell this late, as I have and I was able to still get the most out of it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I absolutely recommend this game wholeheartedly; it's been over a year since I've been this immersed and emotionally invested into a game.  The game makes a point, but it's never heavy-handed about it; I really appreciate that, since too many stories of this nature is ruined by the author's soapbox. game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
More of an immersive novel than a game, Orwell begins as a smart and thoroughly engaging experience that accurately captures the dilemma of state surveillance: The violation of privacy is bad and comes with risk, but there are still real threats that motivated the imposition of surveillance in the first place. Within this context, the events of Orwell are situated within "The Nation" - a hypothetical highly developed country saddled with all of the assets and burdens of the U.S., France, the U.K. or any similar nation. Osmotic deserves praise here - they tightly and intelligently create a nuanced setting without overburdening the player.

But the success doesn't last.

As the game progresses, Orwell begins to exhibit a grasping take on modern security that feels naive. The moderated presentation that offered a balanced dialectic fades, and the political messaging of the developers becomes increasingly heavy handed and blunt. None of this occurs in a way that is surprising or unique within the context of the public surveillance debate, it is only disappointing that they couldn't have done better.

In terms of technical game mechanics, while Orwell's gameplay is a slick, engrossing and well-crafted experience - the buyer should not expect any replay value outside of a 3-5 hour playthrough.

Leaving a negative review feels somewhat harsh, although within the context of a 91% positive title, it feels appropriate for balance. It is by no means a bad game - only one that fell frustratingly short of its potential.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
It's okay. I'm really torn on this one. There are aspects that are cool. It does make you feel like you are really part of an all-powerful government spying agency, and it did make me feel guilty for what I did at times, which is kinda the point. So in that regard I think the game achieved what it set out to. 

However, the gameplay wasn't that fun to me. The choices that you are given are pretty mundane, and some of them don't even make sense. I played it while drunk once, and I sat there for like 20 minutes trying to decide between two options, analyzing the semantics, because both were technically false depending on how you look at it. Eventually I just stopped caring and chose whatever struck me at the moment because sometimes there is no logical answer that takes all the facts into account. Your choices do have an impact for sure, but because of the wording of some of the options, it isn't really clear what you are choosing. Given that it is basically a visual novel, I wouldn't expect the gameplay to be amazing. But I would at least hope for some robust choices, and a riveting storyline. Well, while the premise is interesting, the actual storyline involves mostly frivolous details about the characters and their lives without really making me bond enough with any of them to actually care all that much, so it ended up being kinda boring after the novelty wore off, honestly.

Also, I have to say I didn't really find the world they built very believable. They basically portrayed a totalitarian police state world within the framework of our existing politics to some degree, and it doesn't really make sense. For example, the terrorists all seem to be left wing communist types. Fair enough. But they are kinda portrayed in a positive light, like they are fighting for freedom. But really, they don't want freedom, it seems they idolize communist dictators, so they just want THEIR side to be the totalitarian state. Which makes sense in a way, but then why all the rhetoric about freedom? If you want communism, you really don't care about freedom. And they portray the totalitarian government as conservative. Interesting choice, given that modern conservatives are the ones speaking up for free speech and lower taxes and stuff. Oh yeah, and the totalitarian government wants to lower taxes. Umm, okay? If you have a totalitarian government that can rule with an iron fist, why bother lowering taxes? Don't you need lots of money so you can have all these government programs to run people's lives? As a bit of a politics junkie, the way they built the political landscape has a lot of ideological inconsistencies, is basically what I am saying. I'm not saying it's impossible that there would be a conservative totalitarian regime. But that would come with a specific set of beliefs. They wouldn't be pushing for family values for example. Ever read "Brave New World"? Defeating the family and community structures is key to politically subjugating the population. I could go on, but basically, because of the inconsistencies, I found myself being pulled out of the experience.

Also, there is some weird plot point that tries to tie in this semi-fictional, semi-real world into the actual real world? That part is pretty confusing and I think they could have left it out because it doesn't add anything IMO and it just makes less sense the more you think about it. I think they should have gone all in on a completely fictional world, with a completely different society instead of trying to tie it in in weird ways like making the terrorists left wing punk rock vegan types, and the totalitarian government conservative family types, with all the baggage that comes along with those stereotypes. Think about 1984 and Brave New World. I'm pretty sure that the authors went out of their ways to make sure that no political archetypes were projected onto the characters because that would take people out of the story and into debates about modern-day politics. They would have done well to do the same here. Just make a broader point without muddying the waters with tribalism.

Honestly, I would probably give it a 5.5/10. It's interesting for a little while, so I guess it's good that it's not very long. I had no desire to play it over and see different endings, frankly I was a bit relieved when it was over. So, maybe I should be giving it a hesitant thumbs up... But because I'm so torn on it, and the other reviews are so positive, I'm gonna have to give it a thumbs down to get it closer to where I think it should be.

It challenges us to think about the consequences of our actions and the ethics of surveillance in a society that values freedom and privacy. If you like narrative games that make you think, then this is definitely worth checking out.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h3][i]“War is peace. Freedom is slavery. Ignorance is strength.” [/i]- George Orwell[/h3]


Even if you haven't read anything by George Orwell, you've probably heard about 1984. The dystopia the author foresaw has undoubtedly materialized in the modern world, as most readers of the book like to point out. This assertion is without doubt true; even if you only use the internet for personal purposes, there are still a lot of data crumbs left behind. You can never be certain if someone is keeping an eye on your every online move, whether it be a post about a recent vacation, a comment made on a forum, or the address you use to sign emails. 
This is precisely what Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You promises: it is a game about a reality that nobody wants to face but that hangs in the air.

[h3][i]“The consequences of every act are included in the act itself.”[/i] - George Orwell[/h3]

The game takes place in the capital of a fictional country called The Nation, where on April 12th, 2017, a terrorist attack occurs: a bomb detonates in the famous Freedom Plaza, destroying a statue and killing several people. At the same time, the police receive a note containing the first three stanzas of a German folk song called The Thoughts are Free.

In 2012, The Party, a paternalistic government that leads The Nation, passed the Safety Bill, which gave the government complete freedom over citizens' personal data and the ability to spy on them using a surveillance system called Orwell. This is where your involvement with The Nation begins.
You are the first person who has been selected to be an investigator - a citizen outside of The Nation, who will use Orwell to uncover as much data about a person as possible. You are being accompanied by an Advisor, who will connect you to the authorities. 

The plot is essentially a classic detective whodunit story told in five chapters; throughout the game, multiple suspects will emerge, and your job will be to determine each person's involvement and, in the end, find the perpetrator(s) - or is it?
The aforementioned data (which the game refers to as datachucks) gathering is the game's main essence and gameplay mechanic - you have access to a wide range of websites, phones, e-mail addresses, and even computers, where you must find information related to your lead. This isn't a difficult task because the game highlights them in blue or yellow; the latter indicates a data collision, and you must determine which is the correct data.

A few things should be kept in mind with this mechanic: first, it is completely irreversible - once you upload something in the system, there is no way to change it, and the story will proceed accordingly; second, you do not need to upload every possible datachunk - at first, the game forces you to do this, but later you must be careful what you upload; and third, the game is actually a choose-your-own-adventure with a detective façade - given that there are multiple endings, your choices will have a heavy impact on the story.

Orwell's strength is the moral uncertainty it contains. Players will have to weigh the pros and cons of sharing new information with the people they're investigating versus keeping it to themselves as they gather additional evidence. Because of this, players will feel more invested in the game and more emotionally connected to their choices.

[h3][i]“But if thought corrupts language, language can also corrupt thought.” [/i]- George Orwell[/h3]

One of the game's greatest strengths is its immersive and atmospheric presentation. The dark and minimalist art style, combined with a haunting original soundtrack, sets the perfect tone for an oppressive world governed by The Party. The user interface is sleek and intuitive, allowing easy navigation of the vast amount of information at your disposal. Towards the end of the game, the interface will get much more crowded; however, the game displays a red icon next to a document where new data chunks can be found. Furthermore, the game's soundtrack perfectly complements the dystopian atmosphere, with haunting melodies and industrial beats that immerse players in the world of surveillance and control. 

Orwell does, however, have a few minor flaws. As the investigation progresses through a series of data-mining tasks, the gameplay can feel slow at times. Some players, particularly those who prefer more action-oriented experiences, may find these moments tedious. Furthermore, while the game encourages players to take different paths, the overall impact of your choices on the narrative can feel somewhat limited, leaving some room for a more dynamic and personalized experience unexplored.
The length of the game is another aspect of the experience that could be improved. The story is interesting and the decisions are weighty, yet the game is over in a matter of hours and it left me craving for more. The game's depth of topic and potential for replay may have benefited from more content or branching routes.



[h3][i]“Freedom is the freedom to say that two plus two make four. If that is granted, all else follows.”[/i]
 - George Orwell[/h3]

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a fascinating and unsettling adventure that delves into the moral issues raised by omniscient monitoring and the misuse of authority. A standout in the narrative-driven genre, thanks to its engaging tale, accessible gameplay, and morally weighty choices. Even though it's not particularly long and has a few weaker points, it's a must-play if you enjoy engaging stories set in dystopian futures.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a thought-provoking narrative simulation developed by Osmotic Studios and published by Daedalic Entertainment that places the player in the uncomfortable role of a government surveillance operative. Rather than offering power fantasies or conventional heroism, the game asks you to sit behind a screen, analyze fragments of people’s digital lives, and decide which pieces of information deserve official attention. Set in the fictional state known simply as The Nation, the story unfolds in the aftermath of a violent terrorist attack, where fear, public pressure, and political urgency justify the rapid expansion of a system capable of monitoring nearly every aspect of a citizen’s existence.

The central mechanic revolves around the Orwell surveillance system itself, a sleek but unsettling interface through which you access emails, chat logs, social media profiles, news articles, phone records, and private files. Gameplay consists of identifying relevant “datachunks” and uploading them into official investigation dossiers. What makes this process compelling is that not all information is equally meaningful, nor is it always truthful when stripped of context. A casual message, a sarcastic comment, or an old association can become damning evidence once formalized inside the system. The act of choosing what to submit becomes the game’s primary decision-making tool, transforming seemingly mundane interactions into high-stakes moral choices.

Narratively, Orwell unfolds across multiple in-game days, each representing a new phase of the investigation and introducing fresh characters, revelations, and complications. The pacing is deliberate, allowing tension to build gradually as threads intertwine and suspects emerge. Rather than presenting clear villains and heroes, the story thrives on ambiguity. Individuals under scrutiny are complex, flawed, and often sympathetic, and the more you learn about them, the more uncomfortable the process of surveillance becomes. The game excels at showing how partial truths can snowball into irreversible consequences, especially when filtered through institutional authority.

A defining strength of Orwell is its ethical focus. The game consistently challenges the player to reflect on the power they wield and the ease with which that power can be misused. Uploading information feels procedural and routine, yet the consequences are often deeply personal for the people affected. Careers are ruined, relationships collapse, and lives spiral based on decisions made in silence behind a terminal. The game does not present clear “right” answers; instead, it forces players to confront the reality that surveillance systems are shaped as much by human judgment and bias as by data itself.

Visually, Orwell adopts a minimalist, utilitarian aesthetic that reinforces its themes. Interfaces resemble real-world operating systems and investigative software, grounding the experience in plausibility rather than spectacle. This stripped-down presentation keeps attention focused on text, decisions, and implications rather than visual distraction. Sound design is similarly restrained, using subtle cues rather than dramatic music to maintain an atmosphere of quiet tension and bureaucratic detachment. The result is an experience that feels unsettling precisely because of how ordinary and believable it is.

Player agency is a key component of the experience, though it is intentionally constrained. While the overarching investigation follows a structured path, the specific outcomes depend heavily on what information you choose to reveal or withhold. Multiple endings and branching consequences encourage replayability, as players can explore how different ethical approaches alter the narrative. Some may approach the game as a dutiful analyst focused solely on public safety, while others may attempt to protect individual privacy whenever possible. Each approach reveals different facets of the story and reinforces the game’s central question: who decides what is justified when security and freedom collide?

Reception to Orwell has been consistently positive, particularly among players who value narrative depth and social commentary. Many praise its relevance, especially in an era defined by data collection, algorithmic profiling, and online identity. While some may find the gameplay slow or limited due to its text-heavy nature, those willing to engage with its pacing often find it deeply immersive and emotionally resonant. The lack of traditional action is not a weakness but a deliberate design choice that underscores the quiet, insidious nature of surveillance.

Ultimately, Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You stands as a powerful example of how games can explore modern societal issues with nuance and restraint. It transforms data analysis into a dramatic and morally charged experience, reminding players that information is never neutral and that those who control it shape reality itself. For players interested in narrative-driven games that challenge assumptions and provoke reflection rather than offer escapism, Orwell delivers a memorable and unsettling journey that lingers long after the screen goes dark.

Rating: 8/10

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Stop what you're doing.

Stop reading this and buy the game. Now.

For 10 bucks? (I got it for 8 on sale though) This immersive experience is going to blow your mind (pardon the overused euphemism) but really. Wow. This was an absolutely fantastic ride. I do not regret spending my money on this game whatsoever! I think that, given some exposure on both Youtube and elsewhere, this game could get big! And it should! It's absolutely fantastic! I love the art style personally, but hey, that's personal taste.

Let me tell you precisely what you're getting so this review isn't just screaming praise about this game.

While the mechanics are beyond simple, (click various articles and search them for relevant data) it makes you feel really uneasy about delving into people's personal lives, about what it feels like to be in places you REALLY shouldn't be. 

All of the choices you make, each little piece of information you submit, can come back to bite you in the ass. Hard. If I have any tips for new players, don't just submit everything, ESPECIALLY conflicting data!!!! Make sure to read all bits of information and all of the articles in full before you submit everything! That's not just flavor text around the submittable parts, ALL OF IT IS IMPORTANT! And that's really what I like about this game- there's nothing gone to waste. Nothing that's just hopeless. All 'dead ends' are just waiting for the right door to open with another bit of text. It's nerve wracking and I LOVE it! 

I have no regrets on this game whatsoever. I'm more than happy that I bought it and I can't wait to see more (hopefully more excellent storytelling like in this game!) from the Devs. Really now, if you like story based games like the Telltale series of games, absolutely pick this up. What it lacks in mechanics it ABSOLUTELY makes up for in story, atmosphere, tension, and replayability! I'll be starting another playthrough shortly.

review_text_raw:
Great concept, great art, but bad execution.

Even though the game itself has an amazing art style and atmosphere with good ambient sounds and exciting cases, the narrator and instructor is annoying as hell. After every little update a comment box of him pops out and sometimes he just restates the obvious.

Example:
You have to find out what the names of the parents are so you look through their business website. After updating the names he states: Oh, so it is a family business?

In my opinion this and the constant handholding makes me feel like the game is mocking my intelligence. I couldn't play through day 2 because I just got tired of that "search, update, comment, repeat" system.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I bought the game on sale for 8€ and finished the story within 4hrs.

Pros:

+Important and contemporary message in the light of NSA scandals and the demise of privacy in general.
+Choice matters
+Original gameplay offers a new take on the genre of text adventures.
+Nice interface
+Unique design


Cons:

-The hacking and surveilance parts are way off. In a game like this I would've hoped for more realism.
-Even though choice matters you're being guided by your supervisor in the game. You can withhold information from him but whenever I felt like doing that it was a piece of information mandatory for the story to continue. At 2-way story-forks the most interesting option often was missing I felt, which again lead to the feeling of being railroaded.
-Almost every bit of information you put into the system is commented by a pop-up comment of your supervisor which becomes a nuisance rather quickly.


Conclusion:

I really wanted to like this game. The theme of George Orwells "1984" is more relevant than ever. However I feel like the games tries too hard to hammer home their point of everybody being "frameable" by using one unforseeable plot-twist after another, which again is due to the supervisor railroading you. Also I would rather pay like 5€ more and have the tapped phone calls be actual phone calls instead of reading through live transcipts.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw: Orwell fails on a lot of levels. A lot of very fundamental writing levels. First and foremost it gives you a set of tools that allow you to see what people do on the internet and tasks you with finding the perpetrator of a bombing. You're given one prime suspect and as you progress your web of people of interest grows and grows. The principle gameplay mechanic involves choosing which specific pieces of information you choose to report to your orwellian system. Which will change how the game plays out. The first failure comes that it is often very obvious what information is going to affect what, as it is all highlighted in blue, or yellow if it conflicts with another piece of information. This is another problem. The conflict system makes very little sense most of the time. One of the first examples of the system in use involves a personal blog ran by a Person of Interest and an editorial they wrote for a newspaper. They both detail the same concept but with completely differeing opinions on the matter, and these pieces of information are considered a conflict and therefore cannot both be reported. While this specific instance makes very little gameplay difference either way it still makes no sense. Being able to report both pieces of information would have shown (at least to me) his willingness to play whatever side of an issue would get him paid, and could've sowed him as a much stronger suspect later on. Instead you have instances where you handler is confused by information you weren't able to provide them due to it being a conflict, when both pieces of information were true. This creates a very frustrating experience in trying to influence the story and with trying to keep information that is relevant to the story seperate from information that isnt. Another fundamental failing of the story telling is its ending, which if I'm perfectly honest; is godawful. To my knowledge, your choices throughout the game have no impact on the ending. There's just three buttons at the end. Push one for your ending. None of them making  a bit of sense. Right before your ending the perpetrator of the bombings reveals themselves, showing that the previous three chapters had all just been misdirection to make sure no player could possibly guess the real one and they basically say to you the player "And this is why your system doesn't work! You couldn't even figure out I was the perpetrator" When it was the game mechanics and information that was provided to you by the game that made it impossible to determine the perpetrator. They then ask you to take down the system, since you can now see it doesnt work. your other two options are to get a politician associated with your orwell system arrested, or to claim the group the perpetrator belongs to are all terrorists using out of context IMs. If you're thinking that this seems to be lacking a very obvious fourth option then I agree. My first instinct was simply to use the perpetrator admitting to instigating the bombings to get her arrested. As that would make sense, she admitted it to our face and yet there's no option present. Just the three arbitrary ones presented. In the end it was three chapters of intriguing build up for one chapter of letdowns and unguessable twists that completely kill the narrative, suspension of disbelief, and immersion. 4/10

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A great premise that certainly gets you invested, with certain pieces of information you choose to upload affecting the outcome. Whether that's for better or for worse - that's kind of up to you to decide which side of the fence you fall on. The game leaves it very ambiguous about which side is better - the agency you work for, or the people you are surveilling. Tapping phone calls and trawling social media pages lead seamlessly into conflicting news articles into further conflicting text messages - leaving you unsure what to trust as you decide what you should and shouldn't upload in the mismatch of information (because like House says, "People lie", right?)

Some areas are a little point and click, and the call & text dialogue could definitely do with a skip through feature for fast readers. However the story is very immersive and genuinely does have you wondering if you made the right choice. There are three possible endings, but also a number of outcomes for the characters within that based off your decisions.

A solid game (as is its sequel) for the price of ~£7 that has you questioning the price of surveillance for safety.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Big Brother watches you. That’s what they told us back in the days, when it was just some kinda fiction and a fantastic story. Now, in our present times this issue has become like a real problem, especially for someone who believes, that their lives are important as hell and like to play a private card all the time. 

The government can learn about you literally everything, thanks to social media, your online purchases, all the cameras hanging around the city, watching at you, information you provide to your employers when you attend to job, mobile phones you use with a GPS modules, etc. 

It can be a problem for lots of people, especially for some who is paranoid and doesn’t seem to be busy all the time with any kind of work (because, otherwise, they wouldn’t have time for these kind of thoughts). On the other hand, it can be really helpful to identify a threat and prevent some kind of tragedy from a single murder to a massive terrorist attack.

Orwell try to develop this idea. In this game, which presents as a visual novel with its own dystopia universe, you have to identify the threat. You will do this with the help of Orwell, a program, created for surveilling the citizens. The whole job starts when system marks someone as a potential threat and you have to investigate that person. Usually, it all starts kinda mild and innocent - you check the public records and information, that does not require you to spy on someone or even hack it - you will check newspapers, police records, maybe some websites. However, in most situations it’s not enough and you have to dig deeper, checking private emails, phonebooks, chat logs, listening to phone calls all other kind of intrusion to private life.

So,what’s the whole point of the game? While you checking on person’s information - Orwell will highlight the most important parts, regarding your investigation. And your task is to gather all of them into one piece for every profile, every person. If you are doubt in the information you’ll have to disable it, or simply ignore it. For example you found a statement about your victim in some kinda boulevard newspaper - definitely not trustworthy source and if it conflicts with another info you found earlier it will be highlighted with a yellow color. So, it’s up to you, to choose where is the truth and where is the misleading information. But you should keep in mind, that you are the one who is responsible for what will happen next to this person, so be responsible for your actions.

And that’s what made Orwell so interesting to me - I literally wanted to find the real truth, you know, to investigate this to the fullest. I never had this feeling, like yeah yeah yeah whatever, I put this metadata here, this one there, oh, a conflict? Lol, whatever, just let me finish this game. No, it wasn’t this case. I felt like I was so into the cases, to understand, either I am dealing with a real threat, a terrorist, or maybe we just ran into something really serious, where someone tries to set up a complete innocent guy and maybe I should pay more attention here and re-check all the profiles. So, Orwell is more about investigation and your ability to read between the lines where it’s needed.

At this point, some of the players will understand that this is not their type of game. Like it or not, but you seriously can’t control the situation, you can’t change something, can’t help to prevent the damage, which is about to happen. You just simply have to put facts in a right place with a right persons and listen to the comments of your mentor Symes. That guy is simply ridiculous. It starts as a tutorial guy at the start of the game, who has to show you all the basics and teach you how to play, and then after that it stays there for the game to react on your actions. Basically, it doesn’t have any access to the information you gathered, so it can only comment on the newest information you provided and by these comments you have to understand either you move the right or a shallow way. 

Orwell is definitely a blast. It has this unique kind of a gameplay with its deep idea and rich stories for someone, who truly values games as a real art. The combination of twists, turnabouts and all these thrilling moments make this game a great place to spend a few hours, maybe dozens of hours, if you will feel like having more than one run to reveal all the achievements and endings. 

Okay, to sum everything up!
You should grab this game if you:

+ Conspiracy theory lover
+ Love the idea of investigating and matching data and clues into one piece 
+ You want to entertain yourself in a great story game for at least few hours
+ Like to dig to the bottom to find out who is who
+ Fan of dramatic stories with its twists, thrilling moments and surprises

Recommend to avoid if you:

- Don’t get the idea of visual novel
- Not a fan of all these talks that government spy on you and we are all under control.

Now, in our present times this issue has become like a real problem, especially for someone who believes, that their lives are important as hell and like to play a private card all the time. The government can learn about you literally everything, thanks to social media, your online purchases, all the cameras hanging around the city, watching at you, information you provide to your employers when you attend to job, mobile phones you use with a GPS modules, etc. It can be a problem for lots of people, especially for some who is paranoid and doesn’t seem to be busy all the time with any kind of work (because, otherwise, they wouldn’t have time for these kind of thoughts). On the other hand, it can be really helpful to identify a threat and prevent some kind of tragedy from a single murder to a massive terrorist attack. Orwell try to develop this idea. In this game, which presents as a visual novel with its own dystopia universe, you have to identify the threat. You will do this with the help of Orwell, a program, created for surveilling the citizens. The whole job starts when system marks someone as a potential threat and you have to investigate that person. Usually, it all starts kinda mild and innocent - you check the public records and information, that does not require you to spy on someone or even hack it - you will check newspapers, police records, maybe some websites. However, in most situations it’s not enough and you have to dig deeper, checking private emails, phonebooks, chat logs, listening to phone calls all other kind of intrusion to private life. So,what’s the whole point of the game? While you checking on person’s information - Orwell will highlight the most important parts, regarding your investigation. And your task is to gather all of them into one piece for every profile, every person. If you are doubt in the information you’ll have to disable it, or simply ignore it. For example you found a statement about your victim in some kinda boulevard newspaper - definitely not trustworthy source and if it conflicts with another info you found earlier it will be highlighted with a yellow color. So, it’s up to you, to choose where is the truth and where is the misleading information. But you should keep in mind, that you are the one who is responsible for what will happen next to this person, so be responsible for your actions. And that’s what made Orwell so interesting to me - I literally wanted to find the real truth, you know, to investigate this to the fullest. I never had this feeling, like yeah yeah yeah whatever, I put this metadata here, this one there, oh, a conflict? Lol, whatever, just let me finish this game. No, it wasn’t this case. I felt like I was so into the cases, to understand, either I am dealing with a real threat, a terrorist, or maybe we just ran into something really serious, where someone tries to set up a complete innocent guy and maybe I should pay more attention here and re-check all the profiles. So, Orwell is more about investigation and your ability to read between the lines where it’s needed. At this point, some of the players will understand that this is not their type of game. Like it or not, but you seriously can’t control the situation, you can’t change something, can’t help to prevent the damage, which is about to happen. You just simply have to put facts in a right place with a right persons and listen to the comments of your mentor Symes. That guy is simply ridiculous. It starts as a tutorial guy at the start of the game, who has to show you all the basics and teach you how to play, and then after that it stays there for the game to react on your actions. Basically, it doesn’t have any access to the information you gathered, so it can only comment on the newest information you provided and by these comments you have to understand either you move the right or a shallow way. game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What is Orwell ?

Orwell is a game that has managed to make me fully immersed into it, which is something rare, whenever a game makes me Immersed, it automatically makes that game good for me. In concept orwell introduces you into a terrorist situation and you are an hired investigator who must use this new tool called "Orwell" to bring justice to the people involved in this specific situation, the gameplay is very simple, its just clicking and dragging stuff on screen but I'd rather play this and be immersed than play the latest AAA release and fall asleep just 2 hours in, what makes Orwell special is that its a game that every single choice matter, nothing is black and white, for every stuff you do during your investigation, the special traits the supposed terrorist have that you highlight on their profile, to the locations they visited, their personal lives and the people they have a relationship with, all the occurrences that happen during the 5 days the game takes place on, whenever you finish one of the five chapters aka complete a day of investigations theres a lot of consequences, good or not based on what you decided to highlight, since Orwell itself as a program has a imbued browser system and a profile you have to search every corner for information and make sure that youre putting the correct person in jail, theres contradicting information, I for example failed hard on the second day of investigations, I sent the police to the wrong location and because of that a bomb exploded in a public area, killing innocents, something I could prevent and by the end of the game, no matter what you do, we both will always get different endings since theres so many variables at stake and Orwell is such a detailed and immersive game, it makes every decision count. Another thing to add is that the game plays into hard topics that are relevant to our current times and the game does it in such smart way, its not just another pretentious game, its a smart, well-done game. 

Besides the concept Orwell presents a nice soundtrack and a great sense of style, you will always be looking into this program for most of the time but the game uses this environment to show its great artistic design and despite the gameplay being overly simple with the complex way your decisions are taken into consideration, the immersion the game pulls you into and the very interesting way that this game story which Imo was really well done develops, it just becomes a seamless experience, it took me 5 hours to finish and I would gladly replay it again and this time correcting the mistakes I did on my previous playthrough, I think that Orwell is simple an indie masterpiece, it executes its concept with class, add interesting takes into the whole cybersecurity concept and has a simple but engaging gameplay, In my opinion if you want to try something different that stays with you then this game is a must-play, a very memorable and original game.

review_text_raw:
TL;DR: great game buggered by stupid save system. 

Orwell is a great game, no two ways about it. Easy to get into, nice story and so forth. I didn't have a problem with any of those things, however why have I then thumbed it down? 

Simple, this game, like so many others nowadays, have decided that the only save function this game needs is an autosave, meaning there is no way of backtracking, no way of re-doing things. One slip up and the game will laugh in your face and call you a tosser for the rest of the game, because that slip-up meant you didn't achieve what you wanted to do. I know some people are okay with that, they feel it's more immersive or whatever, but for me it is just a huge annoyance. "Realism" is all well and good, but they don't make the chat convos ingame take 5 minutes per post because while that'd be realistic, it's be annoying. For me it is the same thing here and it leaves me unable to really enjoy the game because it screws me over when I can't decide which of the two vague clues are the correct one. 

It is a crying shame, it's a great game but the save system isn't fun for me at all.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game is one of the few I don’t really feel I can fall down on either side. Ultimately, I felt I should mark it as unrecommended because I couldn’t bring myself to give it a thumbs up, and steam doesn’t have a ‘meh, its ok I guess’ option.

The story is, literally as it is titled, an Orwellian style, drama, I guess. Unfortunately the railroading detracts from the telling. 

The game play is actually pretty good and quite well done. As an investigator you’re expected to dig up as much information as you can regarding suspects in a terrorist attack, and then use their connections and the information gleaned to unpick what occurred and who is responsible, with the ultimate aim of preventing another attack. It is actually the limitations that are forced upon you to ensure you don’t get lost, combined with the multitude of ‘coincidences’ and other sloppy writing that only drives the story in a railroaded direction that bring the whole thing down.

Pros:
The game is easy to play, for the most part allows you to take your time reading the information and make your decision. The way the information is presented is also easy to digest and use. 
The characters are each unique and seem quite well thought out with their own motivations and histories. They also have an interesting dynamic that shows the growth, depth, and fading of their friendship as natural friendships have done.


Cons: 
The game opens with a single character to investigate, while that makes sense from a tutorial point, it doesn’t from a story point. This then focus and railroading leading to a contrived conclusion full of plot holes and excuses kinda ruins the game.
The system showcases a really interesting idea for ways to gather and profile information, monitor suspects, and use what you learn to further an investigation. Then it doesn’t let you do it, restricting what you can see to only a tiny window. It makes for a surveillance system that can’t watch anything.
Tying in to the above, we have so much information on the characters, but can’t utilise any of the information we would undoubtedly be able to access as law enforcement. Once again it felt like an artificial restriction, which was most frustrating.

Suggested improvements:
A skip dialogue button. Most of the few hours I’ve racked up were waiting for conversations to end.
Allow the system to access some of the surveyed individual’s data and build the puzzle environment that way.
Allow us to use the system in the ways we feel fit, not just the way that gives the narrative held.
For the love of god, let us investigate more people, more red herrings. Let us be the ones to cross off people from the lists, let us be the ones that decide what’s worth pursuing. 

Overall Recommendation:
This game has so much potential as a story driven and person centred hook. Especially for people who enjoy info hunts or detective style games. I can see it being really expandable with so many story options.
I think if you like that kind of game, this will scratch an itch for you.
But I can’t recommend it in its current state. As it is it comes off negatively and that just spoils all of the good things about it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I tried this game because of the idea of being a surveillance agent. This seemed pretty interesting to try out, so I started by the demo, to check how immersive it was.
Turns out I was not disappointed.
Then I bought the game, and continued. And I was still not disappointed.

I think the only missing things for the game are the voices during the call. Hearing the emotions of the characters through a decent acting would be even more immersive.

Even though the game might seem trivial at first... Don't let your guard down. I did, and I both laughed and raged when I discovered how deceived I had been.

Finishing one version of the story took me approximatively 5 hours, maybe less. There are however probably several more ways to finish the game, and I shall try it again.
Try not to get spoiled, because all the fun comes from discovering the whereabouts of the involved characters.

It is not a huge blow deeply questioning our society, but it's still interesting, and definitely worth the try. Do not expect any action, though, as this is almost some sort of visual novel.

-- 
Helian

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Preface[/h1]
This review is being written before the conclusion of the game in episode five. I've played through the first four episodes a couple times exploring different outcomes, however, as episode five is not out yet I'm not able to comment on the totallity of the story.

[h1]The Machine[/h1]
[b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] has a very close [url=http://www.cbs.com/shows/person_of_interest/]Person of Interest[/url] vibe. The government of the fictitious country has obtained a Machine, or System, that surveils the populous gathering information however it does not act on the gathered information. The idea of the game is that the system, aptly named [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b], isn't able to decern human subtlety, sarcasim, or deciet. As such, the fictious government has [b]outsourced[/b] the task of resolving conflicts in the data, and identifying what is relevant and what is not. You as the player take on this role as an outsider to the country, tasked with sifting through the data that [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] gives you access to inorder to identify person(s) of interest. This is a role somewhat like [i]Person of Interest[/i]'s Harold Finch.

[h1]What [i]Orwell[/i] Is Not[/h1]
I've seen several complaints that the game isn't challenging enough, many comparing it to several "hacker simulators" such as [b][i]Hacknet[/i][/b] or [b][i]UPLINK[/i][/b]. On the surface the concept might seem somewhat similar to games such as these, however, this is not what [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] is. In this game you are not doing any "hacking" or "cracking", that is [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b]'s job. You are more of a data analyst telling a hacker, that happens to be a computer system, what data is relevant and linked to certian people. Treating it in the same vein as other "hacker simulators" isn't fair to the game and if that is what you are expecting, you will be dissapointed.

[h1]What [i]Orwell[/i] Is[/h1]
So if [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] isn't a "hacker simulator" what is it? I've also seen the categorization as a "visual novel" which is much closer to what this game is. The game play is reminiscent of [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choose_Your_Own_Adventure]Choose Your Own Adventure[/url] books some of you might have read as a child. As such, the outcomes that occur in the game depend on what data you choose to "flag" or "link" to someone as relevant. This process will estabilsh relationships between persons of interest that may uncover new motivations, or might change the context of the data you have available. The game is about you being the guiding hand for a surveillance system tasked with preventing & solving crime.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Interesting visual style
    [*]Enjoyable storyline that feels very linear (as it should), but leaves you with a sprinkling of "what if" moments where you feel things could have been different.
    [*]Fairly Intuitive gameplay.
[/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Somewhat short, although there is some replay value if you want to try to achieve different outcomes from prior play through(s)
    [*]You aren't able to link data to someone until [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] identifies it as potentially relevant.
    [*]You aren't able to revise or change "known" data based on new information
    [*]You aren't able to alter "data conflicts" if you find additional information
    [*]No "Save Game" system, uses the idea of profiles instead to allow for differing play throughs
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
The game is a fun and enjoyable experience if you do not have unrealistic expectations of what the game is and what the gameplay is like. It offers an interesting and thought provoking social commentary on the age of information technology that we live in. The game presents the idea of freedom & privacy -vs- surveillance & security in an interesting and fairly balanced way. If you actually think about what you are doing moment-by-moment in the game, you will likely find yourself re-evaluating your thoughts on these topics. That isn't to say this game is going to challenge your views or change your mind, simply that you will likely find yourself thinking about these topics and why you hold your views on these topics.

If you enjoy naritive driven experiences this game will likey fit well in your games library. While there are some things the game could certianly do better I didn't find these issues to detract significantly from the games main draw for me, it's story & premise. I would like to see the game updated with some sort of "Save Game" system that would allow you to "branch off" after each chapter within a single profile. This would make exploring different outcomes easier, howerver, I also can see that this goes against the linear nature of the games concept. The game strives to make you feel like you are participating in the events, that are time bound and as such linear in nature, which have consequences.

Overall I'm enjoying the game and would recommend it to those who enjoy adventure games, visual novels, and mysteries. This isn't really a problem/puzzle solving game (like a "hacker simulator") so if that is what you are looking for you may wish to pass on this game. I definitely recommend it for what it is and I'm really looking forward to the culmination of these events in episode five.

You as the player take on this role as an outsider to the country, tasked with sifting through the data that [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] gives you access to inorder to identify person(s) of interest. This is a role somewhat like [i]Person of Interest[/i]'s Harold Finch. [h1]What [i]Orwell[/i] Is Not[/h1] I've seen several complaints that the game isn't challenging enough, many comparing it to several "hacker simulators" such as [b][i]Hacknet[/i][/b] or [b][i]UPLINK[/i][/b]. On the surface the concept might seem somewhat similar to games such as these, however, this is not what [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] is. In this game you are not doing any "hacking" or "cracking", that is [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b]'s job. You are more of a data analyst telling a hacker, that happens to be a computer system, what data is relevant and linked to certian people. Treating it in the same vein as other "hacker simulators" isn't fair to the game and if that is what you are expecting, you will be dissapointed. [h1]What [i]Orwell[/i] Is[/h1] So if [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] isn't a "hacker simulator" what is it? I've also seen the categorization as a "visual novel" which is much closer to what this game is. The game play is reminiscent of [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choose_Your_Own_Adventure]Choose Your Own Adventure[/url] books some of you might have read as a child. As such, the outcomes that occur in the game depend on what data you choose to "flag" or "link" to someone as relevant. This process will estabilsh relationships between persons of interest that may uncover new motivations, or might change the context of the data you have available. The game is about you being the guiding hand for a surveillance system tasked with preventing & solving crime. [h1]Pros[/h1] [list] [*]Interesting visual style [*]Enjoyable storyline that feels very linear (as it should), but leaves you with a sprinkling of "what if" moments where you feel things could have been different. [*]Fairly Intuitive gameplay. [/list] [h1]Cons[/h1] [list] [*]Somewhat short, although there is some replay value if you want to try to achieve different outcomes from prior play through(s) [*]You aren't able to link data to someone until [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] identifies it as potentially relevant. [*]You aren't able to revise or change "known" data based on new information [*]You aren't able to alter "data conflicts" if you find additional information [*]No "Save Game" system, uses the idea of profiles instead to allow for differing play throughs [/list] [h1]Conclusion[/h1] The game is a fun and enjoyable experience if you do not have unrealistic expectations of what the game is and what the gameplay is like. It offers an interesting and thought provoking social commentary on the age of information technology that we live in. The game presents the idea of freedom & privacy -vs- surveillance & security in an interesting and fairly balanced way. If you actually think about what you are doing moment-by-moment in the game, you will likely find yourself re-evaluating your thoughts on these topics. That isn't to say this game is going to challenge your views or change your mind, simply that you will likely find yourself thinking about these topics and why you hold your views on these topics. If you enjoy naritive driven experiences this game will likey fit well in your games library. While there are some things the game could certianly do better I didn't find these issues to detract significantly from the games main draw for me, it's story & premise. I would like to see the game updated with some sort of "Save Game" system that would allow you to "branch off" after each chapter within a single profile. This would make exploring different outcomes easier, howerver, I also can see that this goes against the linear nature of the games concept. The game strives to make you feel like you are participating in the events, that are time bound and as such linear in nature, which have consequences. Overall I'm enjoying the game and would recommend it to those who enjoy adventure games, visual novels, and mysteries. This isn't really a problem/puzzle solving game (like a "hacker simulator") so if that is what you are looking for you may wish to pass on this game. I definitely recommend it for what it is and I'm really looking forward to the culmination of these events in episode five.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
OK - to start with the bad; the way progression works is, to say the least, not exactly flawless. At multiple times I felt I had no choice but to do the exact opposite of what my intuition really led me towards, because if the story hasn't moved forward in a while, and you've already done everything that seems sensible, you've no real choice but to just take random stabs. You never know what will push the game to move the story forward, and unfortunately it can really weaken the immersion when you're going back to accept data points you had previously ruled out just on the off chance one of them will finally trigger the script to move forward.

Also, it sometimes feels a little restrictive that you are never freely choosing what information to select for processing - rather, you are selecting which of the automatically flagged information to process. So, sometimes it simply doesn't highlight something which might seem important to you, and sometimes the conclusions drawn from the information flagged isn't quite what you expected. To some extent, these can be forgiven as contributing to the theme that you are not entirely in control of the "Orwell" program, but nonetheless, this can also pull you out of the game if something really catches your attention but the lack of a flag is effectively the game telling you to ignore it.

Those minor irks aside, though - I actually thought this game was very good.

The story is interesting, and generally does an excellent job of avoiding lazy narrative tropes or character stereotypes. The combination of inferring information from investigating documents and reading call or chat transcripts as a means of piecing together events is used to excellent effect. Overall, the story is easily engaging enough to keep you invested in the game throughout, wanting to untangle all the details. 

The mechanics, despite the little irks I mentioned at the beginning of the review, also work really nicely on the whole. They feel genuinely fresh and original, and effectively encourage you to keep paying attention while working through a fairly hefty pile of documents.

I also appreciate that your choices make some meaningful differences, and the story is a manageable enough length that upon finishing my first run I immediately started another to try to reach the other outcomes. However, the repeat playthroughs to see the other possibilities play out weren't remotely enjoyable... The amount of identical information you have to grind through easily outweighs any enjoyment form seeing the alternative paths.

So, only worth playing through once, and not particularly long - but for the duration of that first playthrough, it's an interesting game with original mechanics and the story holds your attention.

I wouldn't pay full price, but if there's a decent discount I'd certainly recommend checking it out.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What to say about this game....

You play as a loyal outsourced investigator for "The Nation", and their new security program called Orwell.  The Orwell program is essentially surveillance designed to "keep the people of the Nation safe."  You investigate a group of individuals in an attempt to determine the culprit of a series of terrorist attacks.  Armed with the most invasive software at your disposal, you use every tool to spy on, and hopefully locate, all of the responsible parties.

Personally, it took me some time to get past the eerie feeling that what I was doing to spy on the lives of these virtual people wasn't too far off from what's probably been taking place in the world for a number of years.  This aspect of the game alone can make you feel almost uncomfortable with what you are doing.  However, your contact within Orwell does well, reminding you that what you are doing is for the safety of all.

The game itself, while it is a reading game at heart, does a really good job of pulling you in.  There are plot twists galore, and the game leaves you wanting to see the next piece of information you can dig up.

TL;DR - If you enjoy a dystopian setting, and enjoy reading-intensive games/mysteries, then I think you'll enjoy this game.  It is a short game; only a few hours, but it is definitely worth a few bucks.  I personally hope that they can use this to make a sequel of some kind.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Tries way too hard to be punchy or meaningful, to the point where its intended messages kind of feel spoonfed to the player. Characters in the story and the dialogue between them also feels silly and surreal in an unpleasant way. Having Symes pop up to give his input at every line of info you drop into Orwell feels abrupt and disrupts the flow of the game. This distracts from the gameplay pretty heavily. I enjoy the gameplay itself though. The conflicting information you're given, challenges you to scrutinise small details about the context of the "data-chunks" in order to record the most accurate information. It doesn't do this enough throughout the game though. I've played through to the end of Chapter 4, but I've lost interest and can't be bothered playing through to the end of the game. 

Tl;dr: Orwell makes you feel smart, and dumb, but mostly dumb.
